• *NOCTURNE. Stills still isthe Night ; still as the pause after pain; Still and as dear; Deep, solemn, immense; veiling the stars in the clear 'Trilling and luminous blue of the moonshot atmos- Pha6; , Ah, could the Night remain! Who, truly, shall say thou art sullen or dark or unseen, Thou, 0 heavenly Night, • • Clear o'er the valley of olives asleep in the quivering light, near o'er the' pale-red hedge of the rose, and the lillies an white 'Down at my feet in the green? Nay, not as the Day, thou art light, 0 Night, with abeam Far more dear and divine; Never the moon was blue as these tremulous heavens of

thine, Tu'sing vrith stars half seen and vague in a pallid shine, Vague as a dream. Night, clear with the moon, filled with the dreamy fire Shining in thicket and close, That frum the lamp in his luminous breast the fire-iiy

throws; Night, full of wandering light and song, and the blos- soming rose, Night, be then my desire! Night, Angel of Night, hold me and cover:me so— Open thy wings! Ah, bend above and embrace !—till I hear in the onebird that sings The throb of thy Musical heart in the dusk, and the magical things, Only the Night can know.

DAISIES. !tippling and tossing at every breath Of the random zephyr that passes by, The daisies sway like a sea beneath The deep blue vault of the cloud-fiecied sky Over the billows of gold and white Flicker the shadows and fall the light. • There's never a daisy in all the host Was here in the summers of long ago, And still the fancy, which charms us most Is a haunting whisper sweet and low, Stirring our hearts with a tender strain, "Here are the daisies back again." The same dear daisies we used to cull When hands were tiny and hearts were gay, Gathering them till our laps were fill, Many and many a summer day, • Softly repeating a magic rune, Fringing the petals to time the tune. And here in the midst of the white and gold, Old as Eden yet ever new, Is the same sweet story of gladness,bold Under the sky so wide and blue, • Her face on the daisies shyly bent, • , His eyes on her with a proud content. There may be, far from this hushed retreat, Din and tumult and sordid care; I Somewhere, perhaps, is the drum's harsh be-4 And women kneeling in tearful prayer; There is only peace where to and Ira In the silent meadow the daisies blow. There are always dreams in this toilsome world, Pure as heaven and true as God, Who sends us dawns with the dews impearled, . And scatters the glory of bleermabroad. May the story that ever's both old and new For the lovers here be a dream come true !

The savage lurks so near the surface in every man that a constant watch must be kept upon the passions and impulses, or he leaps out in his war paint, and the poor integument of civilisation that :held him is flung aside like a useless garment A man wrote to his friend in Greece begging him to purchase books. From negligence or avarice he neg- lected to execute the commission; bet fearing that his correspondent might be offended, he exclaimed when next they met," My dear friend, I never got that letter you wrote me about the books."; As one seeking health does not inquire what degree of intensity in heat or cold he can possibly endure and live, but rather seeks for the most favourable climate in which his physical functions can do their best work, so in choosing life employment men should inquire, not what branch they can possibly push ;themselves into by straining every nerve, but in which one they can do the best work and develop their powers in the best manner. Success IN leee.—Dr. Rem Hunter, the eminent surgeon, adopted a rule which may be recommended to all. Wherla, friend asked him how he lad been able to accomplish so much in the way of stedy and discovery in his busy life, be answered, el!ily rule is deliberately to consider, before I commence, whether the work is prac- ticable. If it be not practicable, ledo not attempt it. If it be practicable, I can aceompliela it if I give suffi- • dent pains to it; and having begun, genever stop until the thing is done. To this ruae kowetall my success in life." The Dube of Wellington was at a bell'one night, and, as usual, could not find a partner. Inheriting his father's taste for music, he consoled himself' by sitting down near the band, which happenedto be aremarkably good one By and- by the party broke up, When the other officers present were taken home by their; lady friends, whilst young Wellesley, as he was called, was, by com- mon consent, left to travel with the Wide. Old Lady Adborough en one occasion put the Duke in mind of the circumstance after he had become a great man ; at, which he laughed heartily, while ehe added,with naiveti „ ei We should not leave you to go home with the fiddlers now." The lady herself used toted the story in the fol- lowing way t—e We had a picnic party near Dublin. I took Wellesley to the ground in my carriage; but be was so dull that I threw him over, and bropght back Is beau Cradock—tbe first Lord Howden. All the, other car- riages having started, or 'beiew full,-he had nothing for it but to return with the band. I 'reminded him of the incident in the height of his fame, adding, When I left you to go home with the fiddlers, I 'little thought you would ever play first fiddle yourself!" When nsaya man's friends naturally suppose that he has gone a missing ?—When he has gone a courting. Pad left out of sight. Some one says, "Man is born to rule the world." Yes; but he sometimes gets married. , The best service that we can render to the world is to mend ourselves; if each mends one, all will be mended. Red is used for danger signals on railicbads, and always means "stop." On a man's nose it ought to give the

same warning. . . . There is frequently more pleasure in giving a thing than receiving it. This applies more especially to medi- cine, advice,- and kias. , Policeman: "Now, then, move on. There's nothing the matter here."—Sarcastic Boy: "Of course there isn't. If there was you wouldn't be here." A young man'told his friend that he dreamed that he had struck his foot against a sharp nail. "Why, then, do you sleep without your shoes ?" was the reply. "If I am not at home from the bachelor party to- night at ten o'clock," said a husband to his wife, "do not wait for me," "That I won't," replied the lady sig- nificantly; "I'll come for your: To prevent difficulty, the gentleman managed to be at home precisely at ten o'clock. A gentleman had a cask of American Wine, from which 'his servant stole a large quantity. When the master perceived the deficiency he diligently inspected the top of the cask, but could see no trace of an opening. , " Look if there be not a hole in the bottom," said a bystander. "Blockhead," he replied, "do you not see that the defi- ciency is at the top, and not at the bottom?" A loquacious lady, ill of a disease of forty years' stand- ing, applied to Mr. A. for advice, and had begun to de- scribe its progress from the first, when Mr. A. inter- rupted her, saying he wanted to go into the next street to see a patient; he begged the lady to inform him how long it would take her to tell her story. The answer was "Twenty minutes." He asked her to proceed, and hoped she would endeavour to finish by the time he re- turned. A certainVelsh sexton has a story of one of his pre- decessors who, when his bells were cracked, used to go outside his tower and call the people to church, in the best imitation he could of the familiar °filmes, with these words—" Shen Morgan, Shon Shones, Shon Shen- kins, Shon Shones, Shen Morgan, Shon Shenkins, Shen Shenkins, Shon Shones," and so on, over and over again, until the parson was ready to begin the service. A wittol, a barber, and a bald-headed man travelled together. Losing their way, they were forced to sleep in the open air; and, to avert danger, it was agreed to keep watch by turns."vThe lot fell on the barber, who, for amuseraent shaved the fool's head while he slept; he then woke him, and the fool, raising his hand to scratch his head, exclaimed, "Here's a pretty mistake; you have waked the bald-headed man instead of me." "Yes, stranger," said a traveller from Texas, "I am goin' down East on an important errand. • Don't mind tellin' you that I'm going to be natrried. You can imagine how good-natured and jolly I feel." "Yes; but don't ran feel a little anxiety, a little trepidation;about taking such an important step in life?" "Nary a bit, stranger." "Have you ever been married before?" "No ; but I've been in one fight with Injuns, two scrimmages with cowboys, an' went through four cyclones. I'm no chicken. "We do not admit obituaries," said an editor to whom had been submitted a long paper, commenting on the death of a man. "I thought that you would be glad to print it." "No, it is not of interest to the majority of our readers." "You would think so if you were to read it.' It tells of the death of Jackson Romley." "Who was he?" "The man who always asked, `ls;that so? eve iy time anyone said anything." "Ah ! then, I will receive it. All my readers will be glad to know that he is dead." , The commercial traveller of a Philadelphia 'house, while in Tennessee, approached a stranger as the train was about to start, and said, "Are you going on this train ?" "I am." "Have you any baggage ?" "No." "Well, my friend, you can do me a favour, and it won't cost you anything. You see, I've two big trunks, and they always make me pay extra for one of them. You can get one checked on your ticket, and we'll euchre them. See?" "Yes, I see; but I haven't any ticket." "But I thought You said you were going on this train?" "So I am; Pm the conductor." " Oh!" He paid extra, as usual. Saarcauxe Ittrixs.—l must admit that when castles arrive at a stage of decay similar to that of Pevensey, my antiquarian zeal is not sufficiently strong to counter- balance•my artistic lack of interest. I have never been able to understand the extraordinary delight with which the majority of amateurs seize upon shapeless walls covered with ivy and sketch them. Some years ago I went over for a'clay's sketching to Pevensey, and horri- fied the numbers of artists scattered like mushrooms over the enclosure by turning my back upon the castle and sketching, from the vantage ground of its walls, the church of Ham and its backgrouno of downs; and I found Mr. Davison of the same mind—he ',would have used the castle walls only as a setting to his view of the church, but that he feared the charge might be brought against him that his work was sadly deficient if he omitted a view. To us the noticeable features of the place were the vast extent which the works covered— namely, an ovar having a length of nearly 400 and a width of 200 yards—the massiveness and interesting composition of its walls, the charming views, at either end, of the villages of Pevensey and West Ham, and especially one lo sking west from the ditch under the south wall.--Art Journal. SOME INSTANCES OF MISTAIHN IDENTITY.—About the middle of the last century a certain Mr. Killett was con- victed and executed on the positive oath of a man named Jackson, who swore he had been robbed, Killett's inno- cence being afterwards proved. Anotheeitragical case was that of two men, named Mackley and Clinch, who were executed for the murder of a Mr. Fryer in Isling- ton in 1797. their identity being positively sworn to by Miss Ann Fryer, the cousin of the murdered man who was with him at the time. Yet years afterward; two criminals severally confessed to the crime for which Mackley and Clinch had innocently suffered. Another unfortunate man named Coleman was executed in 1749 for the murder of a girl, Sarah Green, who swore posi- tively to him as one of her assailants, the real criminals being dis2overed afterwards through one of them turn- ing king's evidence, as it was called in those days. Turn- ing from these tragedies to cases wherein the accused person escaped we shall find equally remarkable in- stances of resemblance between different persons. Ail certain Mr. Frank Douglas, a man of fashion in the last century, was arrested on a charge of highway' robbery. much to the horror of his friends, and certainly would have been hanged but for the following providential circumstance. A notorious criminal named Page hap- pened to be caught and brought to Newgate at the same time, and when the victim of the robbery saw him he recognised his real'assailant; the extraordinary likeness between the two men amply explaining his former testi- mony. A similar. case occurred in New York some 40 years ago or thereabouts, which created much excite- ment in that city. A hotel -keeper was charged with presenting a forged cheque, and the bank clerk swearing to his identity, he was convicted. A new trial was, how- ever, obtained, and after the unfortunate man's business and reputation were gone, a notorious forger happened to be arrested, who turned out to be the real criminal, a remarkable resemblance between the two /being once more the cause of much misery to an innocent man.— Cassell's Family Magazine. TALES OF A WAYSIDE INN.—By the town's end, at Wallingford, we came across an ancient-looking place, standing back from the road at the corner of a lane and with a great tree in front, from one of the limbs of which the old signboard creaked. This was just what we wanted, a large house with wings and yards and out- houses straggling about, so that in the dark the place seemed to be of indefinite extent. We stumbled through the low doorway into a long, low room, with some long tables on each side and a great fireplace at the further end, in which, although it was anything but a cold night, there was a large heap of glowing billets. The room was lighted brightly enough at this end by a great lamp and the ruddy firelight, but the other end was in half darkness, for the walls and ceiling were all dark wood ; made blacker by the great dancing shadows that ',. stretched across A:ern. There were a few countrymen : with their tankards by them, all sitting near the fire in , ssome great settles, and while the hostess got our supper ready we got into conversation with them. Two old fellows were holsnobbing together and comparing notes, -and no doubt telling each other the same old stories for ' the hundredth time. One of them was a rare little shrivelled old man, whom we found was the father of the hostess, and the•former landlord. He was sitting in an ancient beaver hat, and wore a long-skirted coat with a yellow waistcoat of prodigious length. He was very communicative, and was evidently endowed with a lively fancy as well as a tenacious memory, for he told us an sorts•of traditions about the house and its history, and some most extraordinary tales about the neighbouring places and the old castle ruins close by. Whenever he told us anything more .extraordinary than common he would clinch his story byleoking round to %lie, crony and saying,'" Ay, and gaffer Giles knaws that too:" The old house, he said, had been theleadquarters of Olirer Crom- well when he took the place. We suggested—,being by this time 'quite inflated with al:tide-book learning—that a General Fdirfax commanded the besieging force, but he wouldn't thear of it, and appealed once more to old Giles. In connectipn with Shis.event he told us apitiful f legend about the White Maiden who, he declared, still ; 'haunted the old castle's site. There was a country girl - whose lover was a soldier in the Parliamentary forae. In a skirmish hew-as badly hurt and was left for dead upon the ground. When his sweetheart learnt this she ran to the field, and found him lying at the point of death. As she bent over him a party of horse belonging to the Royalist garrison came charging di,seetly towards them. The poor girl shrieked, and threw 117:.rself over her dying. lover, but the horse rode straight down en them, and, as, they passed over, a 'brutal trooper cut her down with his sabre where she lay.—English illustrated Araga:ine. THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, AUGUST 29 1885 _ SCIENCE, ART, Sze- A free Meaty, museum, and art gallery has just been okiesied at Oldham, the cost incurred being rather more thwii asxo. The library comprises upwards of 7,000 •Voltime,s. Messrs. Sangster and Co. are preparing an "Annual" ."`Pictorial Records of the English in Egypt; with a full and descriptiv,e Life of General Gordon. The text will be illustrated with 120 wood engravings and &series of <coleured portritits. Two hundred thousand copies of General Grant's book, says the St. James's Gazette, have already been ordered in America: 'Nearly 20 elaborate biographies of the deceased General appeared, it is said, within 24 kours of his death; all the principal publishers in the Eastern and Western States having printed their "Lives" in advance. Prof. William A. Anthony, of Cornell University, Ithaca, New York, has constiructed the largest galvano- meter in the world. There ere four circles, each two metres in diameter. Dr. Guyter and several electrical engineers are engaged in testing by the aid of the gal- vanometer the strength of the current of a powerful dynamo run at 1,200 revelations in a minute. The private library and collection of engravings of the late Mr. Thomas Hayes, the well-known bookseller, of: Manchester, have just been disposed• of by Messrs. Sotheby, Wilkinson, and 'Hodge. The most important lot was a collection of 2.;922 prints and 631 drawings illustrating the fashions in ancient and modern dress in various parts of the word, forming seven 'folio volumes i bound n morocco, Mr. Sotheran was the purchaser of this lot' for £l6O. Mr. .Hayes purchased the collection in an unbound state for £2Bl at Messrs. Sotheby's rooms in April, 1880: It is possible sometimes to derive amusement even from the tyrannies of the Russian censorship. There were recently sent to the censorship the proofs of a novel called "In TroubletiTimes "—those of the Russo- Turkish war. The author,in describing the tent of one' of the Grand Dukes, stated that among its ornaments was "the portrait of a certain actress.' The censor, altered the phrase to "a large map of the theatre of war." The novelist objected that his description was "historical," whereupon the censor replied that "in Russia nothing is historical except what appears in the official journals." Lieutenant Scheutze, of the United States Navy, who recently departed for •the delta of the Lena river, ex- pects to reach the spot where Lieut. De Long's party starved in a fruitless cause, and will reward, in the name of America, those who assisted in the weary search. His intention is to start about the Ist of August for Irkutsk. He will have to travel 6,000 miles on wheels over neigh roads. At Irkutsk 'he will distribute $l,OOO worth of provisions and supplies among the natives' and $1,600 in money among those:who were prominent in servioS to the Jeannette survivors and search parties. He carries also an elegant swort for General Tchernaieff, Governor of Eastern Siberia; four gold watches, 19 gold medals, and 13 specially manufactured rifles with steel barrels. A good deal of surprise has been excited in the scien- tific world by the action of the Science and Art Depart- ment in relation to the chair of Biology vacant at the School of Science at South Kensington by Prof. Huxley's resignation. This professorship was recently put on a firm footing by s treasury minute, and, being worth £BOO a year, might be considered one of the few prizes ,open to biologists. The Treasury minute, too, in fixing the salary, spoke of the ,desirability of encouraging original research; but such encouragement as this chair gave has disappeared, for the appointment has been summarily suppressed. The salary of Mr. Howes, Prof. Huxley's assistant, has been raised from £2OO to £6OO a year • but this is scarcely considered compensation for the abolition of the professorship. FOSSIL REMAINS IN INDIA.--:Mr. C. S. Middlemiss, of the Geological Survey 'of India, reports an interesting "find" of recognisable fossils in the lower Himalayas of British Gurhwal. The fossils consist principally of "corals, belemnites, lamellibranchs, and gasterpods," and are said to be "probably of Jurrassic age." The rock series in which they are found is described as in the main either a grit or a quartzite, with-here and there a tendency to become calcareous or conglomeratin. The fossiliferous bed has an average thickness of about 50ft. only. Beneath this bed lie, unconformably, a set of purple-and-green slates; and volcanic breccia ; while above it lies, also unconformably, a massive blue-gray limestone which is supposed to have its equivalent in the krol limestone. It is admitted that the fossils are not yet fully identified. No recognisable fossils of a pre- tertiary age have Sever previously been found in the lower or outer Himalayan. The present " find," there-- fore, ushers in a new era in Himalayan geology. LIQUID Ft:mt.—The Admiralty have authorised some experiments to be conducted at Portsmouth with the object of determining the value of liquid Biel for the use of ships of war. There are various systems before the world, but the particular system which is to be tried is that of Baron Adelsward. which has been largely intro- duced into the French Navy. The coal oil is placed in a tank, prhere it is raised to a high temperature by steam from the boiler. It is then allowed to pass to the furnace doors, where it comes into contact with a jet of steam and is driven into the furnace, which has'beentpreviously heated in the usual way. The inventor claims that his system is suitable for the propulsion of armour-clads, but the experiments at Portsmouth will be confined to No. 22 torpedo boat, one of the boats of the largest type, which have lately been received from Messrs. Thorns'- croft. Should the trials prove successful, there can be little question of the superiority of the liquid fuel over coal for consumption in these small craft, quite apart from the question of economy. In the first place there will be no stoking required, thus enabling the comple- ment on board to be reduced, and in the next place there will be no necessity for the use of forced draught and the arrangement of tans by which it is produced. ,These are important advantages when the confined space be,- low deck in the torpedo boats is considered.

It is rash to con- clude anything on such no 'conditions, but one thing is clear—that if from a guts of moderate calibre a shot can be fired which shall crush in the side of any ironclad in existence, the work of a shot will be wisely expended in getting rang with accuracy alone; and It may be necessary to make new calculations for the construction of the most efficient type of gun, while ironclads will be considered as far.more speculative investments. A long gun of relatively small calibre and carrying a long shot would seem in such circumstances to be the gun of the future.—Times.

Swine fever, which has done great havoc in the dis- trict of Sheffield, is reported in the valuable herd of 160 animals belonging to the South Yorkshire Asylum, and several have been slaughtered.

Ilsrrun.—" B." asks when is a calf said to become a heifer? It is a heifer-calf till it is weaned; after that it may be called a heifer, but certainly after a year old. In Scotland ktbwould be called a quey-stirk. Some splendid fields of oats have been harvested in different parts of New Zealand, but a crop recently threshed .on Mr. Buchanan's farm, at Cockleshell, in the Tuapeka West district, tops the list of large yields. A I field af 20 acres threshed out an average of 94 bushels to the acre. If prices were anything good, farming in the Tuapeka district would pay well. The results of threshing wheat in some pahs of the United States are reported to be disappointing in respect , of bath yield and quality, but nothing has occurred to affect the markets materially. The promise of the spring wheat crop is generally stated to be loss bounteous than I early reports indicated; but, on the other Inind, the serious damage done by floods and rust is now declared to be confined to limited wean. -' . _ . .

The Chief Inspector under the Dominion Government of the, ranches of Canada has recently returned from a visit to the cattle districts in the Canadian North-West. The cattle business this year has been, he states, excep- tionally successful. He found that on all the well-con- duct.d ranges the mortality of last winter was consider- ably under two per cent. Owing to the exceptionally fine spring and the. abundance of grass, tho cattle could not have been in finer condition; in fact, many of the steers Were fat in the early spring. The number of calves, on all ranges where a sufficient number of bulls have been kept, will exceed 60 per,cent. of the breeding females, which is considerably above the average in any cattle-raising country. As to treatment of milk fever, a New York ;Tribune correspondent says :—" The way to prevent is to feed about two-Ulf-cis rations of fodder and half rations of whatever mess they have been eating for a few days be- fore they come in, and for two or three days after calving feed sparingly with fodder; give no mess at all for the first day or two after, except a half-dozen potatoes or carrots, and take the chill off all her drink for 48 hours after calving. If the weather is hot, keep her in the shade in the heat of the'clay, and she will not be likely to have any trouble." A COIRTRAST.—A curious contrast in the sense of the "fitness of things" is exhibited by two recent pur- chasers of land at Hindhead. It should be mentioned that the poor people of the district make quite an in- dustry of the gathering. Of wortleberries, which they either sell or make intelam for their own consumption. Professor Tynffall and Mr. A. J. Balfour, M.P., have both secured pieces of land in this beautiful district, nearly nine hundred.feet above the level of the sea. Professor Tyndall has built a house to live in, and hehas a large piece of unfenced moorland attached to his garden, and on it he has notice boards to this effect:—" Berries may be gathered, but without damage to the heather." The other gentleman has fenced his tract of land in with iron railings, and at various spots appears this terrible warn- ing :—"Trespassers will be prosecuted according to law, by order of A. J. Balfour, Esq., M.F.:" NOTES ON HEREFOUDS.—The celebrated bull Archibald 6,290, so well known in tho show yards in this country when in the possession of his breeder, Mr. Aaron Rogers, of The Rodd, has been sold for the very high price of £1,200. He was exported by Messrs. George Leigh and Co., Aurora, Illinois, and passed into the herd of Mr. J. 0. Curry, of Aurora. He has now been purchased by Mr. C. K. Parmiee, Chicago, and goes to join that gentleman's fine collection at Des Plaines. The 13reeders' Gazette, Chicago, says :—" Archibald has had a wonderfully suc- cessful career in the show yards of Britain, and is well fitted, both in point.of breezling and individual worth, to do stud duty, in Mr.'Parmelee's excellent herd. 'The bull has been reduced from is ponderous weight of nearly 3,000 lbs., carried last year, until he now scales but 2.350 lbs. Those acquainted with the taak of removing such a wealth of flesh from an easy-keeping beast will under- stand some of the difficulties attending the reduction of over 500 lbs. accomplished with Archibald since his exit from the English show-rugs of a year ago. The bull Pirate will succeed Archibald at the bead of Mr. Curry's herd."—The sale of Hereford cattle from Messrs. T. L. Miller and Co.'s herd took place at Dexter Park, Chicago, on July 22nd. It was well attended, .there being a large number of the best known breeders present. Bidding was rather slow but steady, and the,averages obtained were good. The cattle were a good lot, and in fair con- dition. Eleven bulls sold for an average of £5O, and ten females at an average of £75. A Pnerzer TYPE or Pul.—To furnish a typical guide to farmers, as well as to breeders, a .committee of ex- perts was appointed at the American National Swine- Breeders' Convention, to report on " °general standard of excellence for a hog which shall best meet the require- ments of the market.' The standard adopted represents "perfect hog most profitable to the farmer And con- sumer," and is above or outside of all breeds. It says : —"Such a hog must have a small. Short head, heavy jowl and thick; short neck; ear small, thin, and tolerably erect, but it is not objectionable if it droops slightly forward. He must be straight on the bottom, from the neck back to flank, let well down to the knee in the brisket, and possess good length from bead to ; back broad and slightly curved or arched from the shoulder to the setting on of the tail; ribs rather barrel-shaped; tail small. The hams should be long from the back to the letting off at the loin, and be broad and full; shoulders not so large, and yet sufficient to give sym- metry to the animal; hair smooth, and evenly set on; skin soft and elastic to the touch; legs short and small, set under the body. and the space between wide; a pod depth between the bottom and top of carcass. He must be possessed of a good, quiet disposition, and, as a gene- ral rule, should not weigh more than 300 lbs. or 400 lbs. ' gross at twelve to eighteen months; colour may be black or white, ma mixture of the two. Such a hog will mea- sure as manyfeet from the top of the head to the setting on of the tail as he does around the body, and as many inches around the leg below the knee as he does in feet • in length or around the body, and the depth of the body will be four-fifths of the height:"

A British sailor thus defined the difference between a hurricane and a typhoon: "In a hurricane the wind blows as hard as it can, but in a typhoon it blows as hard as it can and thee gives a jerk." The son of a fond father, when going to war, promised to bring home the head of one of the enemy. His parent replied, " I should be glad to see you come without a head, provided you come home safe."

div.head: TALE.OFA COFFIN.
div.p: A TALE.OFA COFFIN.
Peter Carmichael and Co. was the name of a firm tbat carried on an extensive business as cartwrights and general carpenters in a village not a hundred miles from the town of Ayr.

Peter was a little man about five feet high, and propor- tionally spare in stators. He was better known in the vil- lage by the nickname of " Blaeberry Nose "—so called from the high colour of that prominent pear-shaped organ, caused by frequent visits to the " Corkscrew " purolic-honse, where the boys used to watch for him coming out, and torment him by shoutieff, "Hey, Peter! ye sad get your nose white- washed—Aelaeberry nose—blaeberry nose—blaeberry nose!" and then they would run round the corners, and there wait in ambush for a favourable opportunity to make a new attack. '

The parish minister got Peter to sign the temperance pledge three times; but he always relapsed to his drinking habits whenever he got into company. Be bad been an abstainer for about a month after he had signed for the third time, when one market-day he got up- roerithisly !`fa," and the boys had once more the pleasure of having some sport at Peter's expense, by shouting " blae- berry nose" at every street corner he turned, to which Peter would reply— . ..
"Al blaeb'ry—hle—nokh ye. I'll brain some o' ye if I get—ttle—a hold—hle—o' ye, ye little imps—imp'dentsh blaelcarde."

The minister soon heard of Peter's outbreak, and resolved once more to reclaim the black sheep. Next evening Peter end his partner, Sandy Grant—who represented the Co. In the firm—were after finishing a coffin that was to go to the farm-house of Drumlea, situated about a mile Dom the village, when Sandy observed— Pate, there's the minister, an' dash ma buttons but he's makin' stracht for oor shop." " Where is he ?" said Peter, rather excited, for he had been drinking pretty freely that day again, and would have sooner met his satanic majesty than the reverend gentle- rn " Yosner, he's cumin'," said Sandy, " peggin' up the street, an' he's makin' for here as sure's ocht." " What in a' the wan' wull I dite, &many ? I canna wit eot or he wad see me; an' if I mann bide here there'll be the diel tae pey. Guidsake, he's just at the door; I'll hide in alow the bench."
" :say, nay," cried Sandy, "he micht tee ye—just jump intae the coffin—an' I'll pit the lid oret, an' I'll pit a wee chip o' wild in the alow it tat+ gie ye breath." And in an instant it was done.
Sandy was in the act of serewing down the lid when in came the minister. "Is Mr. Carmichael in?" asked his reverence.
"A —a—no, sir," stammered Sandy,' he's no in noo," and to hide his excitement he proceeded with screwing down the lid on the coffin.

"Do you know where he is ?" "No, not exactly, but I dinna think he's Vera far awa'— tbat is,! dinua ken—he'll be here the 000." "Did he say when he would be back?" "A—a—no! in tack I didna notice him gaun oot, for he was here just a meenit syne." I'll just wait for a little," said the minister, glancing towards the coffin, which Sandy had just left, and again he questioned— "ls there anyone deal in the village?" "Ou, no! it's an auld maid o' anchty-four that deed at Dramlea," replied Sandy, getting red in the lace. "Oh, indeed!" said the minister solemnly, and then asked, pointing with his stick, "For what purpose do you put a piece of:wood under the lid?" Sandy looked in blank bewilderment, and then gasped— "o, jist a habit—jist a kin' o' a habit we've got intae--that's a7-o—a ye—naetlaing mair." He was about to confess the whole affair when to hie great relief hhe minister walked towards the door and leaked in the direction of the "Corkscrew" inn as it expecting I Peter from that quarter. "Is he aff ?" equeaked Peter from the coffin. " Hand your whist, man, hand your whist! or he'll hear ye," said Bandy following the minister to the door. In about ten minutes a horse and cart with two nien— father and son, named Paterson—stopped at the door. "We cam for a coffin that we are tae tak' tae Drumlea," s Id the old man.

I'm thinking Mr. Carmichael is no gob' to come aye; said Sandy to the igainister, without ever observing what the old m.n had said, but the minister said he would wait fore little yet. Sandy thereupon walked up to the rutin with the intention of whispering something to Peter, but to his surprise he found he had fallen fast asleep. Here was dz. Be could not tell the minister to go away, nor did he

like to tell the men that his partner was lying drunk and asleep in the coffin. Ile had, therefore, of necessity to let matters take their course, and proceeded to give the men a hand to carry out the coffin. "It's ver-a heavy," said the old man. "Ott ay," said Sandy; "its made o' the best bug-oak, and it's lined wi' leed forby. Tbe men, not suspecting anything, believed what Sandy had said. It was now getting dark, and they proceeded on their homeward journey along a lonely road, with nothing bet diminutive birch trees and bog holes on either side, never dreaming that they had Pater Carmichael in their company. they had not gone very far when the young man ob- served that he heard something like a groan from the ooffin.
- Tae ewe' wi' yet haivers," said the old man, who was a little deaf. . _ .

" Whisht! said the other; "hear tae that! something i' the coffin. I—l—heard it movin'." The rattling of the cart on the road had awakened the sleeper, who was quite bewildered, and could not conceive what was wrorli He was dazed with sleep and stupefied with drink. He paused for a moment and felt both sides of the soffin with his hands., "Gracious! What's this rhe muttered. "Timmer abune, timmer on baith sides o' me, timmer a' round me! Miehty me, it's a coffin! Am I buried alive?" and he let tot An unearthly yell, and at the same time kicked the lid clean off the coffin and eat bolt upright. The two men took to their heels like scared sheep, and never took time to look what the object of alarm was like, but ran with all their might across the moss. The young man led the way for some time, but suddenly he stumbled and fell into a bog-hole, which made him more terrified than ever. After a severe struggle he succeeded in getting out—minus his boots. Ile now took to his heels again, crying, "Oh, am kilt! am kilt !—.oh !" The old man, who was now in advance of him, on hearing this shouting, thought the foul fiend had got loose and was fast in pursuit. He ran, and ran like the wind till he reached home. He dashed into th• house bare-headed—having lost his hat on the way—his hair standing en end with fright and excite- ment. 'ltiehty me !—preserve us a' !—what's gam] vrrang wi' ye, gaidman ?" said his wife in utter bewilderment. " °ugh! I see'd a ghaist !" was all he could utter, for he was quite out of oreath, and sank helplessly into the chair. "A ghaist !" she ejaculated. " Whaur was't ? What did It dae tae ye? Ye look as skeered like as if ye had seen a' the decyils in Pandamonia, Mv hert looped tae ma vera mou' the meenit ye cam' sprauchlin' in." She was here stopped by the appearance of a being all bespattered with 111038 and mud, without hat or shoes. " Heeven be aboon us! what in a' the war's this ?" she screamed, and brandished the poker over her head, when a voice cried out— " flinna, mither ! dinna; it's me !" "Guid preserve a' leevin' mortal ! is% you Archy ? Hey ye seen the ghaist tae? What are ye staunin' glowerin' like a half-droon'd doug for there? Whales your bolts an' yer bannet ? an' siccana mess ye hat made o' yer brew white breeks. I think yersel' and yer (either hae gane clean gyte a'thegither ; but let's hear what's like the matter wi' ye." "Wee!, ye see," replied Arehy, " ma faither and me was comin' hame with the horse and cairt, an' I heard somethin' like a body breathin' very hard in the coffin like he was gaun I to be ehokit, an' I telt ma faither an' he wadna believe me. The neatipeenit up flew the lid wi' a bang, and up sttild a goblin-like thing. .1 never seed sic an onyearthly-lookin' ehiel' in a' my born days. I thocht it was the deevil hisser." At this moment the sound of a cart on the road attracted their attention, and all three assembled at the door. As the weird-looking thing drew near they could see by the dim light of the moon that there was somebody sitting up in the cart.

"By a' the pooers o' darkness ! it's the ghaist that's driving, or I'm a glaiket idiot !" esclaimed the old man, gazing in the direction of the supposod phenomenon open- moutherf. "Atehy, get ma gun, and the dong, and the hatchet"

Here each proceeded to arm himself for the defensive, and they were not in a hurry to come back again, each giving the other the preference to lead the van. Peter Carmichael, when he came to his senses and found he bad been deserted by the two men, suspected the truth, and drove on. When he reached Paterson' house, and found that he could make good his escape unnoticed, he left his horse and cart at the door, and quietly turned home- ward. In this manner be evaded ridicule, and at the same time involved the ithole proceedings with a mysterious air of the supernatural.
At length Paterson, followed by his wife and son, cau- tiously opened the door, and, on seeing the cart without a driver, the old man exclaimed-7- ..

"Gracious gnidnessl here's the cut, but where's the driver? He's glen us the slip; he's vanished in smoke, mist likely—if he's—" "Gogh! I seed his held !" screamed his wife, and all three rushed into the house again. "Man but ye're a big cooard. awa' oot and face it maser," she said, although she had little intention of doing go. This, however, nerved the oht man, and he sallied forth once more, to make the discovery that there was noting in the cart but the empty eclair), while his better-half viewed the proceedings with the air cf a conqueror--at a respecta• diatance.—From Ben Brierley's Joined.

div.head: DYNAMITE (4fTNI AND bITE.
div.p: THE DYNAMITE (4fTNI AND bITE.

The fearful ravages wrought by the explosions of dynamite leave no one unable to conjecture *hat might be the consequence of a bombardment in which missiles charged with dynamita should be employed. The diffi- culty has also been easy to anticipate. The shock of explosion of the gun-charge would under the old system ' in all probability fire the shell-charge, dynamite being easily exploded by mechanical shock, and the gun and shell might naturally be expected te destroy the gun- ners rather than the enemy. The Americans, who seem rather fond of trying the supposed impossible, first be- gan to experiment on dynamite missiles, and an officer of the American navy contrived whet may be called a colossal air gun, in which the shell charged with dyna- mite might be started on its flight with an easy but ac- celerating nio4on, avoiding the shock so certainly pro- ductive of premature explosion, and obtaining by a high air pressure through a long bore the velocity requisite. The idea had been foreshadowed by the Lyman accele- rating gun, which, starting the shot with a small charge, followed it up by successive explosions of accelerating charges placed along the bore, and giving it the highest initial velocity ever attained by any gun. The Lyman gun failed, as mi„oht have been anticipated, through the weak spots introduced into the system by the mechani- cal arrangements for securing the accelerating charges from exploding prematurely or not exploding at all, and the great relief given to the gun by the modification of the explosive qualities of the powder has probably put an end to the experiments in accelerating charges. The success of the experimental air gun in throwing to effec- tive distances shells filled with dynamite or even nitro- glycerine was such that a gun of Bin. calibre and calcu- lated to throw a Shell three miles was planned. It was perfectly correct in theory, and was made apparently on the only safe method; but while the scientific officer who conceived it was following out the development of his system by mathematical calculations, one of the more characteristic practical inventors had attacked the pro- blem from the other side. Instead of making his pro- pelling force more elastic, he gave the elasticity to his missile, and by a wad or cushion,. of caoutchouc of the requisite quality so took the first impulse given by the -1 exprosion that a shell filled with dynamite was fired with complete safety and an effect which can be ima- gined more easily than calculated. A shell fired from an ordinary battery gun and carrying 111 b. of dynamite, striking a ledge of gneiss which formed the target, blew out a cavity 20ft. in dameter and 6ft. deep. No fuse is required, as the shell explodes by concussion as it hits its mark; and it was easy to perceive that a single shell , of this description, striking the side of tho most solid I ironclad in existence near the water line would be likely to send her to the bottom. Thus far no. accident is re- ported in the experiments, which are to be, if they are not by this time, repeated with guns of much heavier calibre. But the calibre of the gun is of secondary im- portance; its range and the capacity of the shell for carrying dynamite are the chief elements to calculate on, and if a shell carrying 100 lb. of the explosive can be fired from one of the heavy guns now in use, the first hit decides any conflict as between single ships, and one of our steel unarmoured cruisers will yield no quicker than the Inflexible to the shock of such an explosion. The prospect of suck a change in the condition of war- fare is 1 appalling, and the only consolation which civilisa- tion can raw from it is that it is always the defence that profits most. It is true that comparatively small gunboats carrying one large gun might approach by night, or even by day, near enough to a seaport to throw several dynamite shells into an inhabited city, and with a devastating effect which recent events can suggest, and the boats themselves being small and swift may be very difficult to hit, while the city can hardly, be missed; ' but the land defences have not only the faculty • of ' employing heavier artillery and of :longer range, but of working with much greater accuracy and safety and much less expense, as an acB- - with dynamite, such as premature explosion of a shell, will sink a ship, but would be attended with but slight damage to works or men in an open battery; and such aecidents will always be more likely to happen at sea than on shore. A flotilla of small unarmoured boats, each carrying one heavy gun, will, thus armed and aided by shore defences, defy in defence any ironclad fleet that can be formed to-day; and as the boats and guns ' are already in existence, any rifled gun being available, ' as the entire novelty is in the shot, it is possible that we may see ironclads out of fashion, and the navies of the whole civilised world running to the opposite extreme from that lately resorted to, and building the smallest

But the change in the young men of to-day in Ng; is beyond brief description. They are casting aside garb of their fathers putting their clothing aside v haT ilw the feudal customs oethe country • many of them stepped out of their Sowing robes' into the fashions 0. Western civilisation, and while occasional ludicrous cos! Itrasts are visible we still find a display of tote which I'9 !creditable. Some of these men are leaders of the ptrici; gressive spirit in Japan; and in motley throngg, railroad carriage, and on the steamboat, we meet studfn,. toraif "needve tfh-Ypellstresschtioesolss of Eduroseapercahinngd Arrerrcat InNv:li.llll°°9; abilities are being drawn out for the welfare of tur-A. - country.

BERLIN, WEDNESDAYT—The Imperial Court has rejected the appeal made by the counsel for the defence against the death sentence passed upon Lieske, the murderer of police °facer Ruropf. at Frankfort. KRSIIISIMI, MOM:Ult.—The Emperor and Empress of Austria arrived lure to-day, and were received with manifes- tations of the utmost enthusiasm. The town is gaily deco- rated, and every precaution. has been taken for securing the comfort and safety of the imperial visitors. The apartments prOpared for the Russian Imperial family are gorgeously, furnished., bait those occupied by the Emperor and Empress of Austria are very simply fur- nished. Kaumsza, WIONESDAY. Theatrical and musical per- formances were given last night In the Archiepiscopal Pal- ace in honour of the Russian. imperial guests. The Em- peror, in Russian uaiform, conducted the Czarina to the ball, being followed by the Czar and Empress, while Arch- duke Karl Ludwig gave his arm to the Grand Duchess Marie Paulovna.

BOMBLY, THIIRSDAY.—The Bombay Gazette to-day an- nounces that the Secretary of State for India has sanctioned the establishment in India of a military college, constituted on somewhat the same plan as the Royal Military College at Sandhurst.

EXPULSIONS FROM GERMANY. VIENNA, SllNDAY.—Expulsirins from German territory continue, and the situation ot affairs is becoming grave. Al- ready some 20,000 persons. including 4,000 Jews. have ben expelled. The Neue Free Pressestrongly condemns the mea- sures that have been adopted, and demands the interference of the Austrian Government.

THE .DEATH OF OLIVIER PAIN.—PROPOSED AN 11.-ENGLIS El DEMONSTRATIONS. - PARIS, SATIVIDAY.—SeveraI of this evening's journals state that at the instance of M. de Freycinet, Minister for Foreign Affairs, steps are now being taken to discover the residence of Selikovitch, the author of the letter ta the Intransigeant regarding Olivier Pain's death. but that up to the present all search has been unsuccessful. Sir J. Wale. ham, First Secretary to the British Embassy, has communi- cated to M. de Freycinet a telegram which be has received from Mr. Egerton, dated Cairo, Angust 21, giving the sub- stance of a telegram from Major Kitchener with regard to the circumstances of Olivier Pain's death. The telegram states that Pain went up the Nile in the spring of 1884 in order to join the Mandi, but was obliged to return to Hal.a and Esnsb. In the month of July, however, owing to the great iufluence exercised by the inspector of the French sugar factories at Ermont. Pain was enabled to make a fresh start for El Obeid, where he arrived last year. lie then joined the Mandi at Rahad, but did not accompiny him to Khartoum, and died last autumn on the White Nile while on his way to Omdurman. This account is confirmed by several independent witnesses, whose names are given by Mr. Egerton. With regard tor Selikovitch, Mr. Egerton stales that he was in the employ of the British army, but was dis- missed for irregularities and bad conduct. Major Kitchener declares Selikovitch's account of Olivier Pain's death to be ' absolutely false, adding that he never received any irstrec- dons from his Government concerning Pain, ner did be over I attempt to secure,,the person of , tho French correspondent I The batransigeont announces that a public meeting will be held in the Salle Rivoll on the 36th hat., under the preei• Idency of M. Rochefort, in order to stigmatise the condtict ef the British Government, and protest against the attitude of the French Ministers with regard to the Olivier Pain affair. Other meetinus are being orgmised with the same object. The Intransigeant also publishes insulting articles of the same kind as those that have already appeared itt its columrs. To-day it more particularly threatens Lord Wolse- ley. Sir Evelyn Wood, and Major Kitchener. Pants, MONDAY.—The following semi-official note is pub- lished here this afternoon :—" The British Embassy having made the necessary inquiries in regard to the alleged as- sassination of Olivier Pain. and the British Chargé d'Affaires having communicated the result of the investigation to the French Government, the m ttter must he considered as closed. The dispute is, therefore confined to the conflicting statements of Selikovitch and liaj3r Kitchener, which it is for them to reconcile."

Pears, Mormag.—Baron de Ring called at the English Embassy on Saturday to express ofiletally,- In the name of the French Government, the deep regret It felt at the infa- -1310113 outrages against the Royal Family of England and the British Ambassador which had been printed in the Intransigeant. He said ho was ashamed that such scurril- ous attacks shenld have been published by any French newspaper. This spontaneous expression of regret was fully anDrecia'ei by Sir John Walshman, who, in entuol'- ance with instructione received from the English Foreign Office called this afternoon at the Val d'Orsav to express officially the satisfaction felt by hr Majesty's Ministers at the step which bad been thus spontaneously taken by the French Cabinet.

FRENCH SYMPATHY WITH SPAIN. PARTS, TUESDAY.—The French are taking advantage of the difference between Germany and Spain to give vent to their anti-German feelings. The papers are mod in their praises of Spain. and call upon her to res;st the grasping pretensions of Prince Bismarck. They pretend that Ger- many will give way if Spain only keeps a bold front. They talk of a Franco• Spanish alliance. The lan,nage of some of the papers is particularly offensive, and causes uneasiness BANK ROBBERY IN AUSTRALIA. MELBOURNE, TURSDAY.—A robbery was committed last night at the branch of the Federal Bank of Australia at Hotham, a suburb of this city, when the sum of £2,800 was abstracted. The clerk who slept on the premises was not disturbed by 60 robbers. MELBOURNE, WEDNESDAY. The police have arrested the clerk who slept on the premises of the Hotham branch of the Federal Bank of Australia on the night of the rob-1 liery. He confessed to having taken the money, and in- formed the police that he bad buried it. The greater portion of the sum has been recovered. GERMANS' AND THE CAROLINE PLANDS. DEMONSTRATION IN MADRID. MADRID, SUNDAY.—During the dornonstration this after- noon several persons climb.d up to tbe balconies of the offieial residence of the Prime Minister, and planted he Spangh flag there. Some confusion was cursed by this Incident, but order was quickly restored. The People are perfectly tranquil this evening. MADRID, MONDAY. Simultaneously with the great dethonstration here yes erday popular manifestations against the German occupation of the Caroline Islands were held in the chief towns of several provinces.

MADRID, MONDAY.—111 RIARy &Teets, yesterday, angry cries against Prince Bismarck, Germany. and the Mans were heard. This excitement bias been kept up by the no less excited tone of the Press. The moat outspoken are the Ministerial papers. which are delighted to see that the cholera panic. the financial embarrassments of the Treasury, and the sanitary anarchy in the provinces are all forgotten in thenitated turmoil of the patriotic demonstration here and in other towns. The Opposition journals vie with the Ministerial in advising the rejection of all compromise. The uncou4itional surrender of the Caroline Islands is urged on all sides. Some papers aro so far as to blame the Govern- tnent for not retaking the islands by force. The military journals express the hope that the commander of the Spmieh expedition will pall down the German flag end , hoist tha Spanish instead. or" perish in the atterept.' Any one daring to ask what Spain will ultimately do if Germany alim fires up and keeps the Carolines is immediately charged with Want of patriotism. The people and the papers really talk aa if war were about to break out. Many of the papers urge the early conclasion of the treaty of commerce with England.. THE CHOLERA IN SPAIN AND PRANCE. THE ROSES AND THE LILIES OF THE FACE, AND SOAP. FAMOUS ENGLISH, IRISH, AND AMERICAN BEAUTIES. - One of the gallant poets of France wrote of Mary. Queen of Scots, that her complexion was " clear as a hen's egg with a blush on it" and it is certain Elizaheth was as jealous of Mary's wonderful transparency of complexion as of her claims to the English throne. That lovely but wicked Countess of Essex who compassed the death of Sir Thonaaa Overbary was also noted for her Clearness of skin. The celebrated Irish beauties—the three Misses Gunning —all of whom married Dukes, are said to have had com- plexions so transpartnt that when they rode over the "Lady's Mile," what was passing around them could be seen in their faces as in a mirror. They left Dublin with a five-pound note and two silk dresses among them to take London by storm and the wits of the time averred the last words of their lather on leaving were, " Your faces are your fortunes ; be victuons, be modest, and don't be afraid. of soap." Georgina, Duchess of Devonshire, preserved her charms far beyond middle age and her lovely complexion to the last. Georgina was a Whig, and a warm partisan of the orator Charles James Fez. for whose sake she permit- ted one hundred electors to take a gold coin from between , her lips with their teeth. This was bribery and kissing at the same time, and Fox was returned at the head of the poll. When asked by the Prince Regent where she ob- tained the roses sod the lilies on her, face, the answer was, Soap furnishes one, your Royal Highness, and water the other." Our American women of today have attained to the perfection of severe Grecian beauty of feature, as the Paris- ians, those modern Athenians, are willing to testify, and were their complexions as bright as their faces are classic, would throw the English countenances far in the shade. Perhaps Cnticura Soap will aid them in achieving this triumph of art as well as nature. Mrs. Virginia Fiske, who died a few months 'ago in Balti- more, had a beauty strictly American, now recognised as a distinct type. She was acknowledged to be the most fascinating woman at the Tuileries when Napoleon 111. was in hie glory. The Countess de Castiglione was the belle of Paris before Mrs. Fiske appeared above the horizon. Madame Mariscal ode Laura Smith, of Baltimore, wife of the Mexican Secretary of State, is an American blonde of the patrician type. She is a more beautiful woman than either MrseLangtry or Lady Lonsdale, but not being pro- /visional, her name is not noised abroad no much. She met the Shah of Persia in Paris in 1859, and so captivated his Majesty with her overpowering beauty that he at once offered to make her second in command among his wives. Declined with thanks. Though she refesecl his hand in marriage, the lovely American accepted from the successor of Cyrus A highly perfumed paste or soap, used extensively In Persia, the land of roses and sherbets. This soar), until then thought to be used by the ladies of the Shah's harem only. wnp found, when analysed, to nossess several of the same properties as Cntieara Soap. The perfame of the Eastern sawn cle toilette is more powerful than that of the latter, but not so agreeable'. In skimming the cream of American beauty, we must not forget Miss Mary Anderson. who has so completely vanquished the Cockney heart, much to tile chagrie of Miss Chamberlain and Mrs Cornwallis West. 111 iss Anderson is essentially of the Americin type. Her com- plexion is unique and absolutely perfect, and than she no one is more willing to acknowledge that ehe owes her spiritual appearance, in a great measure, to the free use of Caticura Soap, which has been a favourite with her since it was discovered, or rather recovered from the lumber store of things and arts that have from time to time been lost. Among other lovely, women of face and figure of the purely American type, are Miss Van Rensealaer Cruger and Miss Langdon, of New York, both with European reputa- tion. But, in truth, the mention of any American city as containing fair women par excellence is invidious when Baltimore, New Orleans, and San Francisco are considered, not forgetting Brooklyn, of the resthetic in style. It is strangely characteristic of civilised human nature, that it prefers to be considered as having inherited to having made fortunes, and on the same principle to having been born beautiful to having cultivated beauty. This weakness ac- counts for the few reigning belles to be found as frank as the Duchess of Devonshire and Miss Anderson. That beauty can be cultivated to an extent little dreamed of by those who have heretofore liboured only to destroy it, by the use of poisonous washes and powders. is established by the testimony of thousands of betutitul women, who have relied solely upon the Caticura Soap. Upon this point Dr. Bladgett, a noted authority on the skin, in his recent comparative analysis of skin soaps. Ur"— ‘.This soap contains, in a modified form, the medicinal properties of Cnticura, combined with delicate and fascinating flower odours. " It purifies and invigorates the pores of ' the skin, and imparts activity to the oil-glands and tubes, thus furnishing an outlet for unwholesome matter, which, if retained, would create pimples, blackheads, rashes, and other complexional disfigurations. " Its gentle and continuous medicinal action on these natural lubricators of the skin keeps the latter transparent, soft, flexible, and healthy, and prevents or cures rough. cracked, or scaly skin, aid speedily lessens tan, sunburn, freckles, and other discolourations. • " Hence its constant use realises the fairest complexion and the softest and whitest skin within the domain of the most advanced scientific knowledze Co supply. It is admir- ably adapted to prheerve the health of the skin and satin of infants and children, and to prevent minor blemishes or in- herited skin diseases becoming chronic, if used from the mo- ment of bi- th. "In conclusion, lam obliged to say that an unprejudiced, critical examination shows it to be the highest tyoe of a pure Medicinal skis soap. in which etatementl-am joined by' the analytical chemists of the State of Maestchtteette." The epinion of scientists that there is in nature a subtle essence, possessing curative and beautifying properties. Is thus confirmed, and whether this essence is concealed in the baths of Clermetra. the supposed philters of the almost immortal Nipon de the Jorden water of Madame Rachel, or the now world-renowned Catictrra Soap, it is an inestimable blessing when utilised for the general good.— Harper's Bazar.

"No, sir," he said to the captain, ",r am not sea-sick; but I'm disgusted With the motion of the vessel." , A robustious countryman, meeting a physician, ran to llido behind a wall. Being asked the cause, he replied, "It so long since I have been Sick, that I am ashamed to look a physician in the face." Waste no time in cherishing vain dreams, indulging idle speculations, or in giving way to depressing emo- tions, but resolutely throw them off, and engage in whatever actual work appears most pressing and im- portant.

If that was true, and the opponent.. did not attempt to contest it, he wanted to know how in 33 et. 34 years, if things went on as they were going on now, and populatioa doubled, they might pro- vide themselves with fair and reasonable ease with suste• nance. He had arrived at the conclu+ion that that could only be accomplished by the most rigid economy of every kind so far as the industry ef this greet district was con- cerned. They must be economists in every possible way ; they must cheapen as fat as they could the bringing of the raw material, and they must also cheapen the delivery of the manufactured article when they had to send it Gut, and it occurred to him that no greater economy' in the manufac- turing industry of this great community would be found then in the canal (Loud applause) Sir GILBMIT GREENALL seconded the resolution. He said: Gentlemen, Alderman Burgess did most clearly and distiectly read to you tbe resolution which it is my great pleasure entirely and cordially to second. Mr. Adamson, it is to you on this occiteion that I would addreas myself. I have not been an indifferent spectator, so to speak, during the very severe contest in which you have been engaged. (Hear.) I congratulate you most cordially upon your suc- cess, and I think we have reason to be proud of the admir- able and fair manner in which you have fought the mest severe contest that man could be engaged in. (Applause.) Everyone does most clearly and distinctly appreciate and admire a man who enters upon a contest, fights it nobly and fairly, and who never descends in the contest to strike unfairly, or to strike a blow below the belt—(laughter)---of any man with whom he is engaged. I congratulate you, Mr. Adamson, upon your success, and I do most earnestly hope and desire that as you have been successful in the Par- liamentary contest that you have fought, that you and your enterprise, I cordially desire, may be successful in the future. I have never spoken ores word spinet the project of the Ship Canal. (Hear, hear.) I cordially and heartily desire its success, and as far as I am concerned no action will be taken whatever by me that will in any way whatever impede its program.. (Hear, hear.) All I can say, and all I wish to say upon this question is thia : that! come amongst you to-night willingly and with pleasure. I express definitely and clearly that I have no antagonism in any way whatever, but an opposite feeling, towards the success of this great enterprise, and that I shall be found as ardently as any amongst you here desiring the /MOMS of the great enterprise. (Applause.) The resolution was then carried amide; cheering. Mr. Anamsore, replying, said he thottght they should have been very remiss had not they come to Warrington to acknowledge their obligations for the interest Warrington had taken in the matter and the generous support it gave —support that, coming from the great half-way house be- tween place aud place, acted in a very encouraging, !manner while they were fighting the battle. It was true the enter- prise was a Manchester Ship Canal, but he could not hdp thinking that if there was one district that would be more benefitted by it than another, it was Warrington. He had often thought that if it had not been for the generous and vigorous support so powerfully given by the city of Men- cheater, and the boroughs of Salford and Warrington, they would not have been able to fight so well the battle they had fought, and neither would their statements have been re• ceivad with the same power and support. He largely attri- buted their success, not only to the efforts of the promoters, their engineer, and soliciters, but to no small extent to the tremendous support given by Mr. Marshall Stevens. He never even sat uneasy in his chair when he heard that gen- tleman cross-examined by the Billingsgate cross-examiner, whose language was more becoming a bar parlour or a fith market than a committee. He honoured and respected every true advocate, but when an advocate condescended

to use mean and despicable langnage ; when he acted the part of a decorated mountebank, be most be treated as such. In acknowledging the resolution he thought he should do so on the behalf of Warrington as well as on the behalf of the promoters, for Warrington'a support had been generous and effective. When they were told the story ef the polling in Warrington every member of the committee who heard it was impressed with the fact that the people were in favour of the scheme, and that they should be listened to with respect. Mr. Adamson then gave some statistics as to the committee work, remark- ing that as Warrington had given so much support to the scheme, the towns-people hid a right to be satisfied that the promoters had won on the me-its or their . ere, and that Warrington might congratulate herself, as well as Salford and Manchester, on contributing so well by furnishing the sinews of war. The promoters had fought until they got the Royal Assent to the bill, and now they aeked the people to subscribe like men to the enterprise, and net to alloW the few who had jeoprdised their fortunes to perish, and look on and laugh, and say what fools they were. Let them help the movement and they would have a canal, improved trade and commerce, and the settling amongst them of new man- ufactures. If they would support it with their money as they had done with their voices, he thought there would not be much need to Day interest upon capital. They must go to Parliament and get permission to pay interest upon capital if it is necessary, but he did not think that that would be. Their interest was to make the canal, get their money with the least possible expenee, and invite as few middlemen as possible. (Hear, hear.) Would it not be better to pay for actual work that would be remunerative to every subscriber, rather than that it should be handed over to middlemen? If Lancashire was resolved and was supported by Cheshire and Yorkshire, they would have the money. and the satisfaction of knowing that not one shilling had been thrown away on those who did not give good return for their money. The canal would bring new works to be carried on by the rising generation, without which they might have to go to some foreign land, or per- haps learn a few tunes on a musical instrument and fight for their bread at German railway stations, or some other place at which to get a living. (Laughter.) They had had it established that Liverpool had command of a traffic of 16 million tons per annum in every direction. They did not want to injure Liverpool, but Lancashire had suffered, and if the present system was allowed to remain, what would become of Liverpool when her trade had disappeared? Liverpool then would also disappear. But such a thing must be prevented. The question was one between man and man, and the men who told them that the scheme would not I pay were either holders of railway shares or Mersey Dock I and Harbour Board bonds. These people said that it would , not pay because they had other interests in view. When the matter was put to trial they got the bill because they had a good cause, with plenty of solid truth that no man, however skilled in fibbing, could contradict. He was mak- ing arrangements for the running of steamships, and they were not going to let Liverpool have all the passenger traf- fic. They would take them up at Warrington. and deposit them at Canada. (Laughter and applause.) They must not be surprised to find in a few years three Atlantic liners departing from Manchester and three coming into the saint port every week. (Hear.) It would be a dishonour to the country, if they let this scheme drop after so great an ex- penditure had been incurred. Moreover, by helping it for- ward, they would not only be helping themselves hut the surrounding districts. (Hear, hear.) The canal could he made and finished in less tban four years, and all the busi- ness which Was anticipated would, he was sure, come upon them, and indeed more than they apprehended at present. Wherever there had been an improved waterway there hart been an improved commerce. (Loud applause.) Mr.. LEADER WILLIAMS, who was next calletupon to speak, was received with cheers. He said that he sould be much rather making the ship canal than making a Speech ; It was much more in his line and he thought he could see many in that room who could help him. If ever there was a working man's question this was one. In our little Island great sums were raised, but in how many cases were large amounts sent abroad. If the capitalists of England could send money abroad, it would be hard on Englishmen, and upon Lancashire men above all, if they could not pro- vide the money for the scheme for which Mr. Adamson and his friends had spent years of work, not for their own benefit, but that of the country in which th-y lived. Re- garding the work, it was proposed to give them large docks at Warrington. close to the town, admirably situated, with a tide that would not interfere with work, and they would be able to have manufactories springing up on its banks, which would bring fresh means for the improvement of the working classes. (Hear, hear.) Their enemies said that the work would be a difficult one but they must not believe it. It was said that the Suez canal would never pay, but now there was no better investment— it was so good that England had invested millions of money in it. When M. de Lesseps was in Manchester he (the speaker) was talking to him of the Panama Canal, and he said "Your canal is child's play to what I have got to do at Panama." It was a simple, easy thing, without engineer- ing difficulties, and was really only a matter of pounds, shillings and pence. That morning a large contractor, who had undertaken great works, after going into the estimate., said " I'll do the work for that money." There was no doubt about the sufficiency of the estimates. They were made three years ago, when labour and materials were dearer than now, and there had been very little alteration made. In 1883 they fought his estimates, and his answer was that he produced estimates made by the very men who gave the evidence, in which they were going to do similar work for less money. rhere had been five committees since, but they had not touched the estimates. If ever there was a district in which a great waterway would pay, it was the district between Liverpool and Manchester—(applause)—where numerous factories could be built near to the canal. He had no doubt that with such facilities shipbuilding would follow. Besides the trade at large ports there would be a great local trade on the hanks of the canal. Look what a great chemical place Manes was, anti the proprietor of one of the we, es there told him that 200,000 tons a year was the weight sent out of his works. Waterways had one great Advantage over other systems. If on a railway the trade was doubled so were the working expenses, but if the trade on a waterway was doubled the cost was hardly at all increased They did not wear out water. Once get the canal and they had an absolutely indestructible road. (Applause .> Alderman BAILEY (president of the Manchester Society of Engineers) also made an eloquent speech, in the couse of which he referred to the rise of the cotton industry in Lancashire, and gave several amusing instataces of the op- position that former great industrial enterprises have had to contend with.

Mr. H. BODDINGTON said he was proud to have followed such a noble man as Mr. Adamson. He had fought teir battle famously ad he deserved all the credit they gave him. Warrington, Mr. Boddington went on to say, might be said to be the pioraeer in that great movement, as more than a century had elapsed since Warrington men took up the question, and one worthy successor at least re- mained with them in their enterprise to-day, a replesenta- tvie of a family which might be termed the good patron of that town and a pattern of nobility and worth—he spoke of the Wilson Patten family. NOTES BY THE WAY. The return match with Surrey at the Oral last week closed the important fixtures of the Lancashire County eleven for the present season.

During the past week the averages of the county batsmen and bowlers have been made up for what are termed the im- portant matches, but on the face of it this is unfair, seeing that in those averages such counties as Derbyshire and Che- shire are included, while Essex is kept out. Yorkshire was last week put second in the struggle for the possession of premier county, having to submit to a 49 runs defeat at the hands of Middlesex. The victors, on account of the holiday season, were enabled to put a stronger team in the field than usual. It is in many quarters stated that the Yorkshire team, in consequence of working so much together, is getting rather stale. This idea is fast gaining ground, and the poor exhibition of the Tykes lately is considered to go to prove that a change in a cricket eleven is as good as anything else. Sussex defeated Gloucestershire within five minutes of the time for drawing the stumps by four wickets. In the match 1,074 runs were obtained for 39 wickets. After this defeat Gloucestershire met Surrey and won by nine wickets. The weather, especially on Saturday, helped them greatly in this, as the sun, after the heavy rain on Friday night, rendered the wicket very treacherous. Dr. Grace was in his old form, putting to his credit the respectable scores of 104 and 19 not out. On Saturday Dr. Grace and Woof did their best with the ball and sent the whole of the ten batsmen back between them, the former securing four and the latter six wickets. In the first innings Gilbert was very successful as a bowler, capturing six wickets for 51 runs. Notts now bids fair to once more take up the ctief posi- tion amongst the cricketing counties. On Thursday week the eleven commenced their return match with Middlesex, but the time allowed for it was not Imfficient to see the game played out. This would not, however, have been the case had not the rain interfered. In the first innings each side did well, only 22 runs separating them. In their second innings the Middlesex batsmen fell off, and had the match been played out there can be no doubt hut that Notts would have won. In the first innings the batting honours were pretty evenly distributed all round, while the bowling of the former was well nigh all done by Barnes and Shaw. In their second innings Middlesex did their utmost to ensure a draw. ' Slowtand careful scoring was the rule, Webbs, the usually livel,batsman, remaining at the wickets 2 hours and 35 mintites for 10 runs, and Butler taking out his bat for 17; after a two hours' stay.

LORD CAR/CARTON IN THE NYRST OF IRELAND —A corres- pondent of the Ireeman'sJournal, describing the Viceroy's visit to Arran, says the Viceregal party went into several cabins on the way, and the Lord-Lieutenant made minute inquiry into the condition and habits of the people. Lady Car- narvon was able to hold brief conversations with the women in the vernacular Gaelic. The Lord Lieutenant noticed the exceeding sterile nature of the soil and the absence of boats suflicientiv large for deep sea fishing ; and learned of the inconvenience'arising from the want of a regular steam postal service. The journey. from and to Kilronavne har- bour was made On two jaunting cars, and it was a netts- worthy sight—Lord Carnarcon, without guard or detective, driven through wild and remote Arran by the lately liberated Bryan Kilmartin. Before leaving, the Lord Lieu- tenant requested to have all papers bearing on Kilmartin' care forwarded to him, promising to look into it with a view to obtain compensation for him if possible, I,,rd Carnarvon brought his tour to a abase on Saturday. Replying tolyal addresses at Sligo, he expressed his gratification at the warm welcome he had everywhere received, and said that it was by a kind interchange of feeling and by the begetting of confidence between those who were ruled that the only sure foundations of government could be laid.
