SUPERINTENDENT'S REP32T.—Superintendent Leah sub- mitted Hs annual report with reference to the conduct of the licensed victuallers and beer retailers in that division during the past year. There were 23 lioensed victualler', two beer sellers, and three others who sold off the premises, total 28, which gave an average of 298 of the population to each license. Two licensed victuallers had been proceeded against during the year, one of whom was convicted. No beer sellers bad been proceeded against. Thirty-eight per- sona bad been convicted for drunkenness daring the year, age net 32 in the previous year, increase six. RENEWAL OF LicznasEs.—guperintendent Leah slid be had no objection to the renewal of any of the licenses. All the licenses were accordingly renewed.

APPLICATIONS.—Mr. R. Davies, of Warrington, appeared ' on behalf of Messrs. Greene'', Whitley, and Co., of Wilderui pool Brewery, and applied fora provisional license authoris- ing the removal of the old Saracen's Head public house, which stands at the corner of Wilderspool Brewery, to the opposite aide of the road. The cottages and the garden which are at present at the opposite side of the road would be done away with to afford a site for the new house. At present no estimates had been got Out, but Mr. Owen, archi- tect, who was present, would tell the Bench that the house would certainly cost more than £l,OOO, and accommodation would be made f.sr a respectable class of travellers sad cus- tomers. He might also say that it was in contemplation to give a certain portion of groun3 to the highway if it could be spared from the new building.—A provisional license was granted subject to the old license being surrendered. Mr. Whitlow, publican and farmer. Preston Brook, ap- plied for a seven days' in place of his present six days' license. He stated as a reason for his application that he had applied to his landlord's agent for a reduction of rent, but the latter told him his application would go before the landlord with more force if he obtained a seven days' license for the public house.—The Bench did not think this a suffi- cient reason for an extension, and accordingly only renewed the old license.

SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GOOD TEMPLARY. The quarterly session of the District Council of the Ju- venile Templar Order was held in the United Methodist Free Church, Whisten, on Saturday, when there was a good gatheriog of delegates from Liverpool, Bootle, St. Helens, Warrington, Widnes, and other places. The chair was occupied by Brother Preston, district superintendent, who said that he feared the reports would show a decrease in numbers, but he had much pleasure in chronicling an Increase. (Applattee.) Last quarter, the numberenf mem- bers returned in good standing was 2,063, this q.unrter it was 2,079—an increase of 16. (Renewed applause.) There were 27 temples in the district, an increase of ene-- " Bootle's Hope, Senior "—and the "Sunbeam," of Widnes, headed the list with 325 members. He thought they might safely say that the district was in a very healthy condition. (Applause.) The Treasurer reported a good balance in hand -On the motion of Bro. Hampson, P.D.S J.T., seconded by Bro2Doeley, D.C., it was unanimously resolved "That,, inasmuch as the Juvenile Order of Good Ternplars has for its object the saving of the children horn the evils of pi°. fi fanity ank degradation, having for its motto MIA, Love. and Purity,' this council sincerely accords to the leaders of the movement in Liverpool for bs protection of young girls its entire arnpathy with tflie object they have in view, and tenders its hearty co-operation.' —ln connection with a seggestion made in the report of the district secre- tary, Bro. Tulloch, it was decided, on the motion of Bro. Hampson, seconded by Bre_ Brockbank, to. recommenl temple superintendents to have three open temple meetings each quarter, to which the Public generally are to be specially invited. Liverpoel was unani- !mously chosen as the next place of meeting- At the close of the busin.sa, the members of the order, to- gether with a large number of juvenile templars, all wearing regalia, and headed by the City of Liverpool Good Tetnplar Brass Band, under Brother Craig, walked in proceesion to lialsnead Park, the seat of Captain Willis,J.P., to which I they were especially invited as a private party, aril where they were entertained at an excellent tea by Mr. Ward and his daughters, all of whom were specially thanked. After- wards an open-air meeting was held in the village, and ag.. dresses on temperance were delivered to a large and orderly getheriog. This was followed by a public meeting ia the United Methodist Free Church, whin was well filled. The chair was .occupied by Brother Preston. D.S.J.Te and speech., on temperance politics were delivered by Brother Hampson, Brother J. A. Smith, who was formerly an actor,„ and others. A literary and musical entertainment was also given.

div.head: STEP CANAL.
div.p: THE STEP CANAL.
PUBLIC MEETING IN THE DRILL HALL, WARRINGTON.

On Weelnesday evening a meeting was held in the Mill Hall, Warrington, in furtherance of the Man- chester and Liverpool Ship Canal Scheme. The chair was occupied by the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), who was supported on the platform by Mr. D. Adam- son (chairman of the committee of promoters). Mr. Leader Williams (engineer of the canal), and several geutlemeu from Manchester and Salford, amongst whom were Alderman Husband, Alderman Bailey, Alderman T. Bradford, Mr. W. Fletcher, Mr. Mar- shall Stephens (provisional manager), Mr. A. H. Whitworth (secretary), and Mr. A. Goodier • the local gentlemen on the pla.t,form were Sir Gilbert Greenell, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, Alderman Burgess, Dr. Gornall, Captain Reynolds, Councillors Green- ing, J. Pierpoint, Hutchinson, Tinsley, and Mackie, Mr. Nicholson, Mr. G. Woods, and Mr. Longdin. There was a very large attendance, the front part of the hall being crowded. Dr Mamas, in proposing that the chair be taken by the Mayor, said that now that the fight in connection with the canal was over there was but one suggestion to make, and that was that they might forget all their past disappoint. ments in regard to any of their fellow townsmen ; that V.ey ' ahoeld pass a. act of amnesty and oblivion, and that so far as Liverpool was concerned, a town with which they were so closely connected, they should forget that there had been anything but a straightforward and honourable fight, and that they (the promoters) had been the victors. (Ap- p ause.) Die MAYOR, having taken the chair, said if any proof were wanting that the popularity of the Manchester Ship Canal which had grown from its inception was not diminished, tie thought that the very best proof they could require was the assembly he saw before him. (Hear, hear.) He . . .

, - thought there could be no doubt about it that there must be some vitality in that scheme be withstand as it had with- stood the combined opposition of Liverpool and of the Dock Beerd, an opposition which would have been suffi- cient to have annihilated any scheme that had not real backbone in it. (Applause.) The scheme, however, as they knew, had withstood that oppoiition and had success- fully passed the Houses of Parliament, which was a very important thing, ss it went far to prove that the Man- chester Ship Canal scheme was not only a feasible one but one likely to produce incalculable advantages, at all events to this part of Lancashire. (Applause.) He was sure he was speaking the sentiments of everybody present when he said that if the construction of that canal should injure Liverpool they would he exceedingly sorry for it. But he did not see that it would injure Liverpool ulti• mate's,. A great city like Liverpool was not to be snuffed Out by simply causing a ship canal to be made between Liverpool and Manchester. He could not believe for one moment that it could be so, but even if it were he was sure that was a question that could hardly enter into their con- sideration. If a tradesman entered into business in a town he may do so with the certainty that he must injure sotnp- body, but then they knew that self-preservation was the firet great law, and if the canal injured Liverpool it was one of those unavoidable things for which there was posi- tively no help. He was sure the promoters of the 6hip Canal had no such intention or object as to injure Liver- pool. Thera was no antipathy to Liverpool, and he himself had the highest possible resp,ct for that city and its man- agement. (Hear, hear.) Their friend Mr. Adamson and the other gentlemen from Manchester, who were promoters of the scheme, be had no doubt were very proud of the honour which in so great a measure belonged to them. Whilst, however, he (the Mayor) was willing that they should almost monopolise the honour, he hoped at the same time that Mr. Adamson aad his coadjutors would give Warrington a little credit for having participated, and ex- cellently too, in endeavouring to obtain the success of the bill. (Heir, hear.) He thought that his two predecessors, Mr. Crosfield and Major Pickmere, had both oontribuled to the bill. When it was first introduced they were anxious that the IA! eheuld be carried to a eueoessful issue, and , there were other geutietiled Ville had 5180 participited in it and felt a very warm feeling in favour of it. He did not think their friend Dr. Mackie should be paseed over. (Hear, ' hear.) He had worked most industriously in order to popu- larise that scheme if it required popularising, but its own inherent virtues seemed to have recommended it almost in- stinctively to the consitleration and sympathy of the public; at the same time Dr. Mackie had done a great deal for that canal. Only the other dale he saw a letter in one of the Manchester papers signed Warrington, in which the writ-r said that notwithstanding what he had already done, he was quite willing to put down another thousand pounds under certain conditions in aid of the promotion of that canal. When he (the mayor) came to inquire into it he found that The writer of that letter was their friend Dr. Mackie. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) There had been a good deal said about that Ship Canal being forestalled. They were told that there was nothing whatever to prevent Liverpool and its merchants from erecting cotton mills in the immediate neighbourhood of Liverpool, and by that means checkmate the Minchester Ship Cana/ scheme. That was all very well in theory, but he waa inclined to believe in practice it ' would be found extremely difficult of application. (Hear, hear.) Nature seemed to provide in some mysterious way which he could not explain that certain localities should be peculiarly favourable to certain branches of industry. Man- chester, Oldham, Ashton, Stalybridge,and some other towns had been remarkable for the spread of the cotton industry. How was it that the cotton industry had taken such deep root in those places, and seemed to have kept clear of Liver- pool? It did seem to him astounding that In days gone by manufacturers had not erected their cotton mills within a mile or two of Liverpool, and so save car,iige and other expenses which at present they must necessarily entail. If it had been feasible he was of opinion they would have done so long ago. He was speaking to a Manchester merchant the other day upon that question, and he said they might rely upon it that the Liverpool people could not do what they threatened to do. There was a humidity in the atmosphere of Liverpool that was antagonistic to the manufacturing of cotton. (Hear, hear.) If their reasons were urged for the purpose of throwing cold water on the canal scheme he be- lieved they would be found to be a mere bug-bear capable of very rapid extinction. (Applause.) In conclusion, the Mayor referred to the services of Aldertnan Burgess, whose name was greeted with loud applause, in connection with the ship canal There had, he acid, been no truer friend to that scheme than Alderman Burgess, and he was as well entitled their thanks as any gentleman, except, perhaps, ; Mr. Adamson. (Loud applause.) Alderman BraGESS,wbo was received with loud applause said it was his great good fortune to have had placed in his' hands a resolution which he should submit to them, and which he was quite sure would have their earnest and hearty approval. It had been his privilege as nearly all of them knew to have been deputed by thd Town Couscil of this borough to represent them in the committee-room of the House of Commons along with one or two other mem- bers of the Corporation, and he bad bad opportunities of seeing the zeal and the indefatigable attention that bad

been"paid by the promoters of that: scheme to everything pertaining to it for the whole of the long time that they had been fighting that great battle. The resolotioe be had to submit he would read at once, "That this meeting begs to tender to Mr. A 'ainson and the members of the Pro- .

visional Committee its sincere and hearty thanks for their extraordinary energy and perseverance in securing the pass- ing of the Ship Canal Act, and to the witnesses, counsel, and other gentlemen who had supported them, its appreciation of their labour?, which so materially contributed
_ to the SUCCMIS attained before Parliament." ( plume.) Re thought they would agree with him when he said a more severe struggle,. or a more _ . . .
determined battle had never been fought the Parliamen- tary Committee-room,. and did think there never had been . .
, circumstances under which gen tl omen wllo were promoting a bill could have been placed at greater disadvantage, but
they felt that they had a cause that was wont:l'A the efforts they had to pot forth; they did not fail in their • ' ' . . . .

efforts, and they triumphantly won in the battle. (Ap- plause.) There was, however' a great deal let to be done t money had to be got, shares had to be talikm up. and he hoped theta would be no lagging among the people of War- rington. who had sustained that Ship Canal scheme so nobly up to the present in contributing, in a fair and proper way to the funds for the construction of that canal. In doing so he felt sure that time would deter- mine that it had been a very satisfactory investment. (Hear, hear.) They might depend upon it that there was no part of the country from one end of the cam] to the other that would be benefited to a greater degree than War- ._ .....
ringtou would. They might take it that that canal would be the making of Warrington to a greater degree than any . .
of them bad yet conceived. lie was perfectly satisfied in
his own mind that when. complete. and in working candi-

tion Warrington would shoot ahead of many other towns at present much larger. (Applauss.) With regard to Liver- pool retaliating by establishing cotton factories, it was all very nice; they had the cotton there, and nobody could raise any objection to it. The Mayor suggested that nature had something to do with that, and he was entitled to go a step further and say that nature had already asserted her- self. Liverpool had tried the manufacturing of cotton, and the attempt was a dead failure. (Hear, hear.) There was .. .
- a celebritted corn mill in Liverpool known as the North Shore Mill, which was originally built to work a.; a cotton
fac:ory. For a onre.ber of .years he .had reason to believe
that timse who meddled with that piece of.husiness suffered
very considerably by it, and he thought he was right in saving that none of their immediato. encerssors would be . . .

found having shares in a cotton mill in Liverpool. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) There were a good many things con- nected with the canal scheme that commended it to their no- tice_ Re would but remind them that the arduousness of the

struggle that there had been had brought forth a leader such as Lancashire with all her fecundity of great men only now and again sees. (Applause.) Lancishire produces great men periodically. It produced Cobden and Bright— (applause)—and that other great mm Stephenson was a very near neighbour, but he ventured to say that they had as great a man as any of these predecessors on that plat- form. (Loud applause ) In Mr. Daniel Adamson Lanca- shire had a eon she was proud of, and history would have to say of him that he was one of the greatest men Lanca- shire had ever produced. (applause ) There was one ob- servation he (Mr. Burgess) wished to make. Mr. Pember, in that great speech of his, the last he made before the closing of the bill, said that within an area of 35 miles around Manchester Exchange there was a population of 51- millions, and if they went 10 miles farther, taking a ra- dius of 45 miles around Manchester Exchange they would have a population of 7 millions, or one-fourth Of the inhabi-

presentative, Lord Winznarleigh, had assisted them peeun- arily. and had given them countenance in the Rouses of Parliament and was ready to support their scheme. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Boddington also referred to the assistance given the promoters by Lord Winmarleigh a steward (Mr. WOW), Dr. Mackie, and Alderman Burgess. ard other local gentlemen. They had had, he said, one or 'two opponents in Warrington. One whe had been on their committee, for reasons best known to himself had left them. They all ad- mired Mr. Henry Bleeklev's great and scholarly but they felt that the action he took was a most unkind Cut. They also regretted the withdrawal of their worthy Alderman Joseph Davies. It was not English to put one's hand to the plough and then look back when things were depressed and the outlook gloomy. (Hear, hear.) Whether Alderman Davies did not think it agreeable to his policy to ride a loosing horse or not he (Mr. Boddington) could not say. (A voice: "That's it," and laughter.) Perhaps these gentlemen's opinions had now undergone a change fer the bet:er, and possibly they might have to again call in the aid of those excellent gentlemen (Laughter.) Mr. Bod- dington also referred to the favourable clauses Warrington had obtained in the Canal Bill, and said he anticipated a great increase in the population and industry of the town. Captain REYNOLDS proposed "That this meeting hereby expresses unaoated confidence in the Ship Canal undertak- ing, and pledges its support and assistance in the raising -of the capital for the completion of the project." Ile hoped, he said, to obtain from the canal a great many benefits. He knew perfectly well as a manufacturer, and they all must know as workmen that the fact of the canal going through Warrington must be one of the greatest things for this town that had ever occurred in their time. (Applause.) Mr. G. WOODS seconded the resolution, which was car- ried by acclamation.
Mr. J. PIERPOINT moved, and Mr. GREENING seconded, a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding, and the meet- ing terminated.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, AUGUST 29, 1885.

. • I What may be called the Confidence Trick Ix' the Tories consists in pointing to certain reforms to which they have been compelled , '") Yield assent, and then asking their open- Mouthed hearers if they have not assisted in carrying measures which have been of benefit , to the people. We know how they resisted the 3.:tension of the county franchise—the Tories to the House of Lords taking up the cue of Tories in the Commons until the country was On the verge of a revolution ; but, although 1 the ink with which the Act was printed is 1 ticarcely dry, they are even now claiming to ; oave " assisted " in carrying this greatscheme ! reform. Such politicians as Sir GILBERT ' ~..`IItEENALL and Sir RICHARD Cftoss find it `°ovenient to ignore the fact that their op- Dosition to proposals for lowering the fran- -1 tc,hise is on record ; but it is to be hoped neY will discover that the electors have good • teMories when they go to the poll. There th,,,of course, no hope for the future from . xf.-se who have done nothing in the past. ,h ' i ..,,e Tories have any good things in store gml the way of legislation, they are very care- ti,-. to keep the matter a profound secret. But "4 much is certain—that when they are I,,tl,tiestioned as to reforms which the working :ass deem necessary, the answers they give -thre utterly disappointing_ Take the case of toe M iners, and the candidates for the New- en, Division Sir RICHARD CROSS and Et2l"el MCCORQUODALE. The miners have copted a Parliamentary Programme ; they aave drawn up a series of questions, and irtinswers in writing have now been received /n-11,1 the two candidates of the Division. b—ue first instance, Colonel McCoaQuo- ALE was waited upon, and replying to the cluestloB which were put to him by the de- PSeuctaretit°anrY,she stated we are quoting the v• w•ould statement—that "if elected, he su 1 oPort every one of them." This i s exceedingly satisfactory to the deputa- I who published the answer along with I -,jengthy epistle from Sir RicRARn CROSS, ' ;.v.tiOSe response was of a wholly different kind It would seem that the Tories, irrita- to find that Sir RICHARD figured so badly, ti?aght to divert attention by making light of r,(le Personal exposition of Colonel McCoß- setrouALE's vies; so by way of putting an d to all controversy on this head Mr. S. ems, who had corresponded with Sir , i ICaLiRD wrote to the Colonel for .his views III; detail on the "Miners' Parliamentary .:°gramme." We publish the reply in ' trother column, and need hardly say that, ,ts ,It is all the miners could desire, it contrasts , ~.(lost favourably with the halting expressions "f Sir RICHARD CROSS. The questions are . Vtuirably framed ; and the electors of the . vewton Division could not be better 4'°em- than in studying the answers which . nwave been given by the two candidates.' They N,lllll soon see who it is that wants reform and , oit is that would shirk it. ,th ‘r~on i relates to a proposal to amend Employers' Liability Act, for which oriel Mc,ConQUODALE says he would tl. prepared to vote. Sir RICHARD • as ()_s dances round the question, and, il +Nile ends by making no promise , ti"tever, it may be inferred that he would ot vote far an amendment of the Act. He te "there seems every reason to expect employers and employed will follow the ' herlqie " set in the counties ‘of Northum- in and and Durham—that is. of loyally carry- the nresent Act. Such an expectation taidicolous. If there were any reason, not pett 3' " every reason," for such "great ex- reo tiolts," Mr BURT would not have been lititt'red to bring in a Bill on the subject, for , as t"av be taken to know the needs of miners if cell as Sir RICHARD CROSS. Asked (2) Illetle will vote for "the necessary amend- of the Mines Regulation Act," Colonel ~..01, Plieit 'QuoDALE answers, with manly sim- shoiL " Yes ; employers and employed Sir D ..' be placed on the same platform." .. CIIARD gives the answer—the stock ase er, when nothing is meant—that if any Matt't haTdshio arises he will "judge of the i° the same impartial spirit in which •seerZe‘t was originally passed." This, as it q th Lc' as, is an insult to the intelligence . e Miners ; their case is that the hard- Continual, and that is why they are hiceng a remedy. As to question 3, Colonel or:„uoDALE says he will vote for "a .Krclik"ga reform of the Land Laws." Sir to - :IP) mocks his questioners by referring " a "make believe " reform as the Lands Act, and asks them to " rest

div.p: content," Yes, "Rest content ; shut your eyes and open your mouths and then see what CAIRNS has sent you." But will they? These miners are not to be put off like chil- dren, and we are quite sure they will not "rest content" to be befooled in this way. With regard to Royalty Rents, Sir RICHARD, unlike the Liberal candidate, will not even vote for a Royal Commission of Inquiry. He is apparently determined that there shall still be occasion to speak of the Tory party as " the stupid party." Colonel MCCORQUO- DALE Will (5) vote for "the abolition of the London Coal Dues." Sir RICHARD will not commit himself to more than saying the matter may become "well worthy of con- sideration" As to question 6, which relates to free education. Colonel MCCORQUODALE promises to vote for amending the present Act, so that poor parents may not require to go before Boards of Guar- dians. as at present, for remission of school fees. Sir RICHARD CROSS asks— Why should I or anyone else have children educated for nothing at the expense of others who, it may be, can ill afford it, any more than have food for nothing. or clothing for nothing, or house rent free ?" The answer is that what is called "free education" would be best for the scholars, the teachers, and the taxpayers. His reference to food and cloth- ing is totally beside the mark. Government does not pay for three fourths of the people's food or clothing ; but it does pay three fourths of the cost of education, and, having gone so far, wise educationists and sound economists, the Miners of the Newton Divi- sion included, have come to the conclusion that it would be best it Government paid the other fourth also. Answering question 7, Colonel MCCORQUODALE shows himself in favour of pqing "a limited number of mem- bers." Sir RICHARD CROSS thinks that those who want " pecuniary assistance" should look to "their personal or political friends without calling upon the public purse." He does not seem to see that it is not a case of begging, but of requiring payment for ser- vice rendeted—after the fashion, for instance, of a salary to the Home Secretary. Colonel MCCORQUODALE gives a definite promise to vote (8) in favour of a bill "empowering rate- payers to pay returning officers' fees." Sir RICHARD " rests content" with the indefinite and common-place remark that "much may be said as to the returning officers' fees, if the incidence of rates be only properly ad- justed." " Much," indeed, may be said, but there needs no ghost some from the grave to tell us this. The last question (9) relates to "a thorough reform of the House of Lords." The Liberal candidate is, of course, in favour of it ; but the Tory member does not go further than indulge in vague talk of "im I - provement in the constitution of that House ;" while he is horrified at the idea of removing bishops—a change which, we venture to say, must be made if there is to be any reform at all. The electors of the Newton Division have now, side by side, the views of the two candidates for their suffrages. If they are half asleep, and ignorant and selfish, they will vote for Sir RICHARD CROSS ; if, On the other hand, they are wide awake, intelli- gent, and philanthropic, they will vote for Colonel MCCORQUODALE.

M. ROCHEFORT, a French journalist who is notorious for his anti-English feeling, has been making a stir of late about the death of a Frenchman named OLIVIER. PAIN, who went out to help the MAHDI. There have been various rumours as to how PAIN passed off the scene; and we know from painful expe- rience in the case of General GORDON how difficult, if not impossible, it is to get an ac- curate account of what takes place in the in- terior of the Soudan. M. ROCHEFORT has always had a theory of his own as to the disappearance of PAIN, and that is that he was murdered at the instigation of the Eng- lish Government. From hinting at the absurd story, he has come to openly affirm it, and has gone so far as to seek to in- timidate Lord LYONS. the British Ambassador to France. More than this, he has suggested that a personal attack should be made upon the PRlNcit OF \YALU on his next visit to Paris, by way of avenging the death of PAIN. This is M. ROCHEFORT'S way; he is always ready to suggest. if not to do. some- thing desperate. By way of giving colour to his theory, he has published the statement of a Polish Jew named M. SELIKOVITCH, who professes to know all about the assassi- nation. He gives details which would be thrilling if they were not, ridicu'ous. "On the 18th of April (he says) OLIVIER PAIN was shot in the desert near Abu Dom by two Bashi-Bazouks, under the eyes of Major KITCITENER. to whom that horrible duty was entrusted. Nobody in the camp was ignorant of these details. Is it necessary to add that this murder was celebrated by a fete, and that the Bashi Bazouks gave a fantasia to the English officers, to thank them for their hav- ing so generously paid the blood money?" Englishmen, to their credit be it said, have never for a moment troubled themselves about this monstrous charge; but there are Frenchmen who would think if nothing was said in the way of denial that nothing could be said, and it has been deemed necessary for the English Government to in- stitute an inquiry. The result is that MAJOR KITCHENER gives the slander a flat contradic- tion, while Mr. EGERTON describes the nar- rative of SELIKOVITCH as an invention. He states that it is known that PAIN died whilst on the White Nile near Khartoum. and he adds as to SELIKOVITCH, that "he was in the employ of the British army, but was dismis- sed for irregularities and bad conduct." with these facts before them, the French Govern- ment have properly intimated that they regard the matter as closed; but M. ROCHEFOR'T will go on shrieking, and he will shriek now at the French as well as the English Govern- ment. The pity is that there should be any section of Frenchmen to give ear to an abomi- nable story which has no better foundation than the imagination of a disreputable foreigner.

MR. I. S. LEADAM, the Liberal candidate for the Altrincham Division of Mid-Cheshire, has just issued two useful pamphlets on The Extension of the Franchise. Their object is to check-mate the Tories in the move they are making to obtain favour with the new electors on the impudent assumption that they welcomed the Reform Bill, and helped it to pass. In the first part, “ How i the;Tories welcomed' t," Mr. LEADAM quotes the speeches of Tory members on the intro- duction of the Bill by Mr. GLADSTONE ill Feb- ruary, zBB. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL said " the agricultural labourer, as a general rule, was absolutely unfitted for the exercise of the franchise. For his own part, he ventured to say that there were subjects of much greater importance which the Gov- ernment had better have dealt with before they turned their attention to the subject of

div.head: EXAMINER SAIURDAY, AUGUST 29.;1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SAIURDAY, AUGUST 29.;1885.

7- Parliamentary Reform." It is clear from this that if his lordship could have had his way the Two Millions would not at this moment have been, as they are, within the pale of the constitution. Mr. GUY DAWNAY, Conservative member for North Yorks, said the " downward extension of the franchise was absolutely dangerous and un- constitutional in the power it would give to one class, and that the least intelligent and least educated class of the people." Other Tory members are quoted as speaking in the same strain. In the second part—" How the Tories helped ' it," Mr. LEADAM gives details from Hansard of the various forms of; obstruction resorted to by the Tories to pre- vent the bill passing. Mr. CHAPLIN, who is now Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. showed the feeling of his party against the Irish by moving "That this House c.onsiders that to largely increase the electoral privi- leges of the Irish people cannot fail, with the present proportion and distribution of seats, to give strength and encouragement in the prosecution of their aims to the Separa- tist party in Ireland." It was in spite, not by the aid, of the Conservatives that the Fran- chise in Ireland was made uniform with that of England. Sir RICHARD CROSS had a way of his own of reducing the value of the Reform Bill. He had the hardihood to move to omit " and lodger" from the words of the Bill, " A uniform Household and Lodger Franchise shall be established." But the House was in no mood for humouring the vagaries of the member for South Lanca- shire, and the amendment was negatived without a division. Numerous other in- stances of obstruction are given. The pamphlets are just in the nick of time ; they are published by the National Press Agency, London, at one penny each, and they are therefore within everybody's reach.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

- - - - THE RECHABITES OF RUNCORN will hold their annual demonstrations to-morrow and on Mond ty next. Full par- ticulars will be found in our advertising columns. TRIP FRO u WIDEES.—About 300 persons travelled to Southport on Saturday by the Parish Church excursion, and the weather being fine passed a pleasant day. CAMDEN MITITAL IstraovEstwr CLASS, Itcscoesr.— The members had their last " ramble" on Saturday, when they were conveyed in a large waggonette from Mr, Peck's to Delamere Forest, where several places of interest were visited.

HOLY TRINITY Dee Scnoots, RUNCORN.—Che 203 scholars who had qualified themselves to take part in the an- nual pic-nic went to Chester on Friday by special train. Under the care and direction of Mr. Annett, the head master, they thoroughly enjoyed themselves in the ancient city. NARROW ESCAPES FROM POISONING AT RUNCORN.—On Sunday afternoon Jane Hassell, aged 9, Sarah Ann Hassell, aged 7, and Mary Jane Smith, aged 10, all living in Mason- ' street, Runcorn, were in the Cricket Field, in Canal-straet, and at a quantity of the peisonous toadstools which grow in abundaece there. On returning home symptoms of pois- oning soon developed, and Dr. McDougall and his eesistant, Mr. Ansbro, were called in. Emetics were administered, and the younger Hassell and Smith quickly recovered, but the elder Hassell, who had partaken more freely of the fungi, was in a dangerous state for a considerable time. She has now recovered. PROPOSED NEW HOTEL AT HALEBANK.—At Woolton Licensing Sesaions, on Friday, an application was made by Nathan Ford (for whom Mr. /Nekton, jun.. appeared) for a fu:l licence for premises which it is proposed to build near Halebank Station, at the junction of the read leading from Hale to the station with the road from Halebank to Hunt's Cross. It was intended to call the new premises the Manor Arms Hotel, Ald as soon as built the applicant would agree to close his present place (the Cock and Trumpet at Dale, one and a half miles away), so that the number of licensed houses in the district would not be increased. The premises would be of the annual value of £lOO, the owners being Messrs. Greenall and Co. The Bench refused the ap- Plication. A HINDI:Er EXCURSIONIST' DROWNED IN TIT 2 MERSEY. —On Saturday afternoon Thomas Bolton, of Stoney-lane. Hindley, a clogger, aged about 24 years, went to bathe in the River Mersey, near the lighthouse at Hale Head. He was accompanied by his brother-imlaw, James Grundy, a collier, also residing at Hindley. After being in the water a short time Bolton commenced to struggle, and Grundy went to his assistance, Belton seized hold of Grundy by the wrist and neck, and as neither of them could swim they sauk,ahe depth of the water at the place being 14 feet. B altoMbecame exhaustel first; and as he let go his hold of Grundy the latter rose to the surface, and, with great diffi- culty, scrambled to the beach. He then shouted to some ' persons who were near, and they assisted him out of the water. A search was then instituted for the body, bat it was not recovered for two hours afterwards, when the tide had ebbed sufficiently. THE SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.—The inquest upon the body of George I'. Littler, grocer, of Surrey-street, I who was killed by falling from the roof of the Market Hall on Friday night last week, was held on Saturday afternoon at the Lion Hotel, Greenway-read. Mr. JE. Worsley, the I deputy coroner, officiated. Evidence was given by William ; Roach, clogger,High-ste W. A. Cashin, a boy from Parker- ' st., and Thos. Williamson, grocer, of 49, Church-etreet, bear- ing out the account published in the Examiner. A verdict of 'Accidental death" was returned. On Monday after- noon the body of the deceased was interred at the cemetery. The funeral cortege was preceded be the Rev. W. Vain, and Dr. Mangan. The procession was composed of about 20 membere of the Union Tent of Rmhabites, attired in mourn- ing regalia, many members of the congregation of St. John's Thesbyterian Church, and teachers, officials, and scholars of the Sunday school, with which the deceased was connected. The body was borne by members of St. John's Bible class, and was followed by the relatives and fiends of the de- ceased, amongst whom were Messrs. George Littler (father), James Littler, Walter Littler, B. Littler, Albert Littler, Arthur Littler, John Littler (brothers). Charles Littler (uncle), Thomas Roach, Wm. Roach (brothers-In-law), Thomas Kirkham (builder). Joseph Ack,rley, J. Gitten, Jas. Richardson, J. E. Richardson. cite. There were also in the procession Messrs. J Pritchard, J. Kirkham, J. Humphreye, W. Leech. F. Hewitt, R Evans, John Evans. R. Leyland, 1 Jesse Leach, Lawrence, Daniel Jones, A Baxter, George i Ellison, George Mort. and R. Harrop. The coffin was covered with floral offerings from friends. The impressive ceremony WAS performed by the Rev. W. Vause in the ab- sence of the Rev. E. Williams, and at the conclusion the large assemblage of mourners sung the hymn " The home over there." The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. James Kirkham. RUNCORN Mcasur MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.—The anniver- sary services in connection' with these missions took place In Runcorn Public Hell on Sunday. During the past year, the missions, ably conducted by Mt. W. Shaw, have done e good work. Both at Sunday school end evening service the , mission room has been inconveniently crowded each Sun- day, .and. the boatmen and seamen present have ectered heartily Into the services. On Sunday afternoon Mr. W. P. Roberts, of Liverpool, delivered a capital address to a large congregation, and in conjunction with Mr. Hobert, his wife sang several solos. In the evening the bui'ding was packed to its utmost limit, and Mr. Roberts delivered another ,earnest address. Mr. and Mrs. Roberts also rendered several solos in their accustomed admirable manner. Mueic spe- cially selected for the occasion was sung by a choir corn- paled of the members of the band, under the conductorship of Mr. A. Jones. Mr. G. Howard was at the harmonium. The collections in raid of the missions amounted to £lO. On Monday the annual excurelon took place. The Liverpool steamer " Fairy Queen" had been chartered for the day and departed from Runcorn Pier at eleveji o'clock with 700 pas- sengers on board. Oa the way to the seaport city a call was made at the training ship " Indefatigable," which was fully inspected by the visleare. On arriving at the landing stage the excursionists were conveyed in 'busses to the North a.ek, where they had the privilege of viewing the White Star Line steamer ' Republic." The Fee Engine Stetion, the Sailors' Home. New Brighton, and other places of interest were visited. At 530 the Sunday school teachers and workers from Runcorn and Ellesmere Fait sat down to an excellent tea provided by the Liverpool committee in the Price-street latieeion. Afterwards the Rev. T. Patrick, char/Liu of the missions, gave the vieitors a warm welcome, and the proceedings were taken part in by the Rev. A. M. Armson, Messrs. T. Williams, W. A. Pearson, W. Shaw (Rnecorn), and John Howard. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the c I aimitteo for their generous hospitality. The excursieuists arrived safely beck at Runcorn at half- past ten.

THE CALRGEB AG.LINST RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS.—The Committee appointed to investigate the charges brought against the members of the Ship Canal deputation has held several meetings this week, and it is expected will report to the Board meeting on Wednesday next. DEATH OF MR. H. F. WHIG, FORMERLY OF RUNCORN. —Oar obituary column announces the death of Mr. Henry Francis Wigg, second son of Mr. Charles Wigg, managing director of the Runcorn Soap an.l Alkali Company. The deceased, who was only 21 years et age, was a partner in the Globe Alkali Works., St. Helene. He died at Llanfair- fechan after a short illness. Flags were flying half mast at the works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, at the Old Quay Copper Works, and the Camden Soap Works.

THEFT FROM A WIDNES PAWN SHOP.—Alice Hall, a mid- dle-aged woinan,was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, charged with stealing eight yards of merino worth Bs, the property of Mr. Collins, pawnbroker. Twaddle subsequently found it in the prisoner's house.— [The prisoner pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to six I weeks' hard labour. .

THE RECENT PRIZE FIGHT AT WIDNES.—On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Peter McCabe, a soldier, was charged with being concerned in the prize fight at Crow Wood on the 19th June, and also with assaulting a labourer named Michael Muroby.—The prisoner pleaded guilty to both charges.—Constables Almond and Moores proved the breach of the peace. Murphy said he was in a house in Warrington-road, when the prisoner came in and gave him a blow on The head which knocked him to the floor, and then kicked him on the ribs.—lnspector Wood said the pri- soner was a very bad character, and had been seven times before the Bench.—He was ordered to find sureties to keep the peace for three months or go to gaol for a month on the first charge, and for the assault he was fined 40s and costs or a month's hard labour. INHUMAN PARENTS AT WIDNES -At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Elizaeth Connor was convicted of deserting her four young children at Widnes, under circumstances already reported, on the 12th instant.-She was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour.—Edward McTaigh was charged with having on the 2nd October, 1884, ran away from Widnes and left his wife and seven children chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Mr. Scannell said on the date named he found the prisoner's family living in on empty house in Pear-street in a state of great destitution. They were removed to the Workhouse, where they had remained until June. The pri- soner eystimatically deserted his family. In five years they had been in the Workhouse three years and two months, and the cost of their maintenance bad been £3lB lOs 01,—The prisoner was sentenced to two mouths' bard labour. Tetanr Hy A FARM SERVANT AT RCNalliN.—John Fever, servant to Mr. Buxton, farmer, Aston Grange, and John Spender, of Sutton, was brought up at Runcorn Petty Ses. sions, on Monday, charged with stealing two horse face brasses, and two brushes, the property of John Rutter, far- mer, Halton Lodge Farm ; one pair of leggings, the pro- perty of Reuben Potter, labourer, and oae whip, the pro- perty of Joseph Clark, labourer. On Saturday night the prisoners, in company with a man named Thomas Higgins, of Preston O'th' Hill, get drunk in Runcorn, and on their way home they entered a stable at Halton Lodge Farm, whore they slept until morning. The things mentioned in the charge were afterwards missed, and the men were fol- lowed. Higgins made a statement which established his in- nocence, and Spender and Paver were taken into custody. It was then ascertained that Pover had sold the leggings to a fellow-servant named Dewnes for Is, and the other articles were found in his possession.—Pover was tined £3, or in default a month's hard labour. Spender, for whom Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared, was discharged MARRIAGE OF MR. F. W. CLARE.—The marriage of Mr. Frederick William Clark, second son of Mr. Richard Clark. harbour master, Weston Point, to Miss M. Grounds, daugh- ter of Mr. W. Grounds, of the Dock Hotel, was solemnised at All Stints' Church, Runcorn, on Monday. The docks at Weston Point and the houses in the village were decorated with bunting, and the deepest interest was taken in the event of the day. Fine weather prevailed, and many per- sons were attracted to the Parish Church to witness the ceremony. The wedding party drove to the church in carriages supplied by Mr. S. Yarwood. The servicewas con- ducted by the Rcv. J. J. Bryant, M.A., incumbent of Christ Church, Weston Point. The bride was attired in a travel- ling dress of ruby silk, trimmed with plush to match. The bridesmaids were Mies E H. Clark. sister to the bridegroom; Miss L. Grounds, sister to the bride ; and Miss E.J. Rosen- berg, niece of the bridegroom. These young ladies wore dresses of cream nun veiling with ruby sashes and hats to match. On emerging from the church the newly married couple were received with showers of rice, while several girls strewed flowers in their path. Mr. and Mrs. Clark afterwards left Runcorn for London, en route for Clovelly, Devoeshire. The presents were very nun,erous. On Tues- day evening the whole of the piermen at Weston Point were treated by Captain Clark to a capital dinner in celebration of the marriage. CRUELTY TO • HORSE AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Seasious, on Monday, John Phillips, servant to Mr. Joseph Seokes,farmer, Halton, was charged with cruelly ill- treating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state. Aboat seven o'clock on the evening of the 13th August, Mr. Greenwell, inspector to the R 5.P.C.A.., saw the de- fendant driving a bay mare attached to a abandry, and On examining the animal he found a taw wound about the size of a florin underneath the saddle. The wound was discharging matter, and was causing the animal much pain as the saddle Dressed upon it. The defendant said "It isn't very much, but it has been a little had for some time." The wound had all the appearance of being an old one.— Superintendent Leah corroborated.—The defendant called a witness who stated positively that when he hernesse4 the horse in the morning there was no wound whatever upon its back.—Mr. Stokes said he was perfectly astonished when he heard of the affair, as he looked at the pony from time to time, and he believed he did se the previous day. There was no wound upon its back then. A shilling-piece covered the wound up completely. The defendant had been in his service fol the past twenty years, and in the service of the family for 40 years, and he felt sure from what he knew of his disposition be would have told him had there been any. thing the matter with the horse. His animals were always well cared for.—Mr. Greenwell said all he had to complain of was the wound.—The Bench imposed a fine of 10s, and coete,l3e 133. Fenn IT FARNWORTH.—ALLEGED INCENDIARISIM—A serious tire occurred at Hanging Beach Farm, Fernwortht occupied by Mrs Ann Rirnmer, on Tuesday. About two o'clock on the morning of that day one of the servants awoke, and seeing that the shit:mon was on fire, gave the alarm. A messenger was immediately despatched to Md. nes for the fire brigade and engine, and these, under the comenand of Mr. J. Carr, the superintendent, were quickly on the spot. Police-sergeants Strickland and Coutts and about 8 constables were also present and lent valuable The efforts of the men were wisely directed by Mr. Carr to preventing the filmes spreading to the other farm build- ings, and although they were is dangerous contiguity this was accomoliehed. The sh ippon with its content aof hey and straw Was entirely destroyed. The damage, which is estimated at £l2O, is covered by insurance. P.C. Almond was walking up Millfieldeimad at the time of the outbreak, when a man came running towards him as though he were pursued, and the constable arrested him on suspicion. From a statement made by this man, named William Torn), another rough-looking fellow named Martin McHugh, was apprehended, and both were brought up en Tues- day, on a charge of maliciously setting fire to the shippon, an were remanded. On Wednesday Martin Mitchell, an elderly man, was remanded on a similar charge. Yester- day tini men, Martin McHugh, Willi am Fean, and Martin Mitchell, were brought before Mr, Holbrook Gaskell, junr, charged with having between one and two o'clock on Tues- day morning last wilfully and maliciously set fire to out. huildines at the Hanging Birch Farm, Farnworth, doing damage to the extent of £lso.—Miss Ann Riinmer said she was the tenant of the farm. The prisoners were employed by her on the harvest field on the 24th met, and she paid them off at night. Foul had worked for her two days pre- viously. None of the prisoners asked permission to sleep in the barn and had they done so she would not have per- mitted them. At half-past nine everything was quite right, but between one and two her manager, Thomas Wainwright, awakened her, and she found the shippon, barn sheds, and lofts on fire. There were six cows in the shippon, and hay and straw and implements in the other places. The cows were removed with considerable difficulty. There was a stable close by in which were two valuable horses. She had had the damage estimated by a competent person, and it wee stated to he £lso.—Thomes Wainwright. the mana- ger, deposed to Foan asking for permission to sleep in the barn. He replied that " Missus did'nt allow anything of the sort," and that if he did not go away the "policeman would have him." He discovered the fire, alarmed the in- mates, and removed the animale.—F. Simcock, landlord of the Blackburn Inn, said when the prisoners left his house at closing time they were advanced in drink hot not drunk. Evidence was given by Inspector Wood and P.C's. Hudson and Almond to the effect that Foul and Mitchell persisted in statements that McHugh struck a match and set fire to A litttle straw. McHugh made no reply to the charge.— The prisoners were committed to the assizes for trial.

THE QUEEN, on Tuesday morning, about two o'clock, passed through Bank Quay railway station. Warrington, en route for Scotland. ASSAULT IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE.—WiIIiarn Gil- mour, house dealer and furniture broker, Strange- ways, Manchester, was on Wednesday committed for trial at the sessions on a charge of having as- saulted Miss Stead, 16. living at Iluddersheld, whilst she was travelling in a train from Warring- ton to Manchester on the 6th inst. The London and North-Western Railway Company prosecuted. Miss Stead says Gilmour put his arm round her waist and kissed her several times on the cheek. Gilmour re- served his defence.

A WIDNES IRONMONGER. FINED.-At Warrington Borough Court, yesterday morning, Thomas Henry Thomas, described as an ironmonger,of Widnes, was summoned for using abusive and obscene language at Arpley-street, Warrington, on the London and North-Western Railway, on the 16th July. Mr. For- rand, of Liverpool, prosecuted on behalf of the Rail- way Company, and Mr. Husband, of Widnes, ap- peared for the defendant, who was not present. A witness named Thomas Baldwin, booking clerk at Arpley station, who was on the day in question acting as ticket oollector, spoke to the language of the defendant, who appeared to have been some- what irritated.—The Bench imposed a fine of 5s and costs. . _

Mn. CHAMBERLAIN'S VISIT TO WARRINGTON— There is every prospect of Mr. Chamberlain's visit to Warrington on Tuesday, the Bth September, prov- ing a great success. Already there is an enormous demand for tickets from Liberals living at a dis- tance who are anxious to have the opportunity of hearing the right hon. gentleman; but regard, of course, will first be had to local requirements. As the Public Hall will not be large enough to accom- modate all who desire to be present at the Mass Meeting, arrangements are being made for an Over- flow Meeting, which Mr. Chamberlain will also ad- dress. A Conference of Liberals will be held in the Co-operative Hall on the Tuesday afternoon, the proceedings to commence at half-past two. It will be composed of representatives of The various Liberal Associations of the Divisions of Cheshire , and of South-West Lancashire, and will discuss various political matters of importance. TORY TYRANNY IN TILE KNUTSPORD DIVISION,— On Thursday evening Mr. J. Emmott Barlow, the Liberal candidate for the Knutsford division, ad- dressed a meeting of electors in support of his can- didature, at Morley, near Wilmslow. Mr. Joseph Wood presided.—Mr. Alexander Bedell (chairman of the Wilmslow polling district) in seconding a re- solution, proposed by Mr. E. Pearson, pledging the meeting to use every endeavour to secure Mr. Bar- low's return*. said the Tories were very fond of pos- ing as the friends of the people, 0,11(1 of the farmers especially, but in going almt the B.uutsford division he (Mr. Bedell) and others found, over and over again, instances where people had been told that if they did not vote for' the Tory candidate at the gen- eral election they would be deprived of their bread and their living. How could it be said, then, that the Tories were the friends of the people? The meeting was a very enthusiastic one. —•

FARNWORTIL AGRICULTURAL SHOW.—The ar- rangements for this annual exhibition of cattle, implements, kc., on Thursday next, are now being pushed forward. and as it is taking place a fort- night earlier than usual anticipations are enter- tained that it will be one of the most successful organised by the society should the weather be pro- pitious. The entries in all classes are good, and the exhibition of leaping and turn-outs is expected to surpass all previous displays. The only draw- back is with regard to pigs. Swine fever is preva- lent in the district, and the animals cannot be moved front one placed to another, and pigs, which are as a rule very fine in this neighbourhood, will be Antirely absent. Mr. IL Whiteside, the courteous secretary, has been reluctantly compelled to return many entrance fees to disappointed breeders. The Hon. Leopold W. 11. Powys will preside at the luncheon, and will be supported by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., and other local gentry. The Widnes Soap Works Band will be in attendance during the day. THE HOME IRON TRADE.—A slight change for the better has come over the English iron market. At any rate, there has been a rather stronger feel- ing in pig-iron, although it is not general. The shipments of iron from Middlesborough beginning to show up more favourably for the current month, it is thought by some in the north of England that the turn of the tide has set in. Last week prompt No. 3 G.M.B. pig-iron was done for 31s 7id per ton, but during the last few days there has been more inquiry, up to 32s per ton having been paid. As if convutced that the lowest price had been reached, investors have been quietly securing iron against the inevitable rise, and the fact of their doing so, it is thought, will by itself help forward toe general movement. At Newcastle a slight improvement has come over the pig-iron trade, and it is hoped that the lowest possible price has been touched, and that the market will continue to mend. No. 3 Cleveland pig is delivered to the Tyne at 34s lid to 34s 3d per ton, after 2s 3d per ton freight and dues have been paid. and No. 4 grey forge quality is bought at 33s 3d to 33s 61—Iron. RUNCORN COMPETITION WITH Mn. PARNELL'S STONE QUARRIES.—Messrs. Brundrit and Co., of Runcorn, have addressed the following letter to the Lord Mayor of Dublin:—" Sir,—Our attention has been called to a report in Friday's paper of speeches made by Mr. Parnell and others at a meeting in Arklow relative to some set quarries. There is no truth whatever in the assertion that the Welsh set quarry proprietbrs combined to reduce prices in opposition to Mr. Parnell. Our prices are regulated by supply and demand, and have varied ss. below and ss. above our present quotations daring the 30 or 40 years we have dealt with the Corporation of Dublin, and during the whole of that time we are not aware that any fault has been found with the quality or mode of conducting our business. We do not enter at all into the question of equality of the material. If Mr. Parnell has something equal to or better than oars, he will find all the towns in Lan- cashire ready to receive his sets, where the English consumer will neither ask whether they are Irish or Welsh if they suit his purpose in quality and price. We consider that the Local Government Board are not justified in advancing money. tothe Corporation of Dublin unless they go to the best market for their sets, nor can we think that the ratepayers will ap- prove of being taxed for the advantage of any individual quarry owner." Tau ELECTION CAMPAIGN.—A London correspon- dent says that the Marquis of Hartington will lead off with an address to the electors of the Rossendale Division of North Lancashire, which the noble lord will, no doubt, represent in the new Parliament. There is somq expectation that this event will be followed by a counterklemonstration on the part of the Tories in Accrington; but as yet no definite programme has been arranged. On the 3rd Sep- tember Lord Randolph Churchill will attend the Cutlers' Feast at Sheffield. and on the following evening address a political gathering in the same town. The noble lord will be followed by Mr. Chamberlain, who will open what promises to be a campaign on his own account at Warrington, on September Bth. A week later the right hon, gentle- man will be in Glasgow, and thence he will proceed to Inverness, where he has a series of engagements to fulfil. He will be followed in Glasgow by Lord Randolph Churchill; and meantime he will have returned to London, where he is engaged to speak on September 23rd. Then on the Ist October he is due in Bradford. at the meeting of the National Federation of Liberal Associations. This will be followed a week later by the meeting of the Na- tional Union of Conservative Associations, who are to have Lord Salisbury to speak to them; and so the talk, once begun, is likely to go on till the elec- tions are over.

.1 A MUDDLE-HEADED PROTECTIONIBT.—A Stock- port gentleman having forwarded to Mr. Bright copies of the speeches of Messrs. Tipping and Jen- nings, Conservative candidates for that borough, who advocate a duty on imported manufactures, Mr. Bright has replied, stating that ML Jennings exhibits himself as one of the most muddle-headed of all the Tory speakers who are now addressing the constituencies. He would not trouble his cor- respondent with proofs of this; but feels sure the Stockport electors will see the folly of the statements of the Conservative candidates. " BAT-m.131.°N RECTORY."—This week's issue of Judy has the following notice of this work, which is having a large circulation in this district :—" Much Henpecked Hushand.—For any man to be hen- pecked, and to know it is very terrible ; but when the lady ii a Mrs. Rector, with an appetite for de- vouring curates—those poor gentlemen who, with the Rector's help, assist her in carrying on the work of the parish—the example is not ednying. Yet all this, and more, is the tale of Battleton Rec- tory;' one of the neat little shilling• orths pub- lished by John Hey ood, Manchester and London. The complimentary speech in which the wretched man's health was proposed at the Mayor's dinner is 'not a bit overdone, and would only seem sarcastic to everyone but himself. From the happy despatch meted out to the curate who dared to fall in love, and a certain hurry in some of the many incidents, I fancy the author is a young hand ; but he has evidently lived in a terrible she-dragon's parish, and not scrupled to paint her in bold colours.,' •

The annual Brewster Sessions of the Runcorn Petty Ses- sional Division was held at Runcorn Pollee Court on Mon- day morning. The msgistrates present were Messrs. inn. Bruodrit, W. Bushes, A. Thomas, James Handley, and G. L. Davies.

div.head: SUPERINTENDENT'S REPJRT.
div.p: THE SUPERINTENDENT'S REPJRT.

Supt. Leah read his annual report, which stated there were 45 licensed victuallers, 52 beersel fere. and seven others who sold oil the premises; total 101. There WA@ an average of 184 of the population to each license. Four licensed victuallers had been proceeded against during the year, two of whom only were convicted. 'fnree besraellers had been proceeded against and three convicted. DI persons had been convicted of drunkenness during the year, against 128 In the previous year; increase 63. No second conviction had taken place against the same publican or beerseller during the year, nor had an endorsement been made upon any of the licenses. lie bad not, therefore, servel any notices of objection. He had thought it necessary, however, to call the worships' attention to those who had been convicted, in order that they might receive a word of earniag.

THE THEATRE ROYAL—THE LICENSE REFUSED On behalf of Mrs. James, of High-street, Mr. Fletcher ap- plied for the renewal of the license to perform state plays at the Theatre Royal. lie remarked that the place had been licensed for 21 years.—Superintendent Leah said last year the magistrates asked him if he had inspected the building, but as he had only been in the town a few days he had no opportunity. He had en the present occasion in•pected the theatre, which is a wooden structure, on the 11th Augast, and presented a report. The main entrance and the only means of egress which appears to have been need for years, is approached by stone steps from Wellington•street, nine feet wide, divided by iron rails, leaving 3ft. 6in. and a door 2ft. 10iu. wit:6 opening inward as the only available en- trance to the front and side boxes, Which seat comfortably. 185 persons. On the left side of the entrance is a Passage live feet wide with a door at the top 2ft. 10in. wide leading to the pit and gallery. seatin, comfortably 677 persons. There is, howerer. another door from the pit opening into a small yard 71t. 3in. by 10t. Sin., but people passing out through this door have to leave the yard by is door 31t. 2in opening inwards on to the sone stew; and would so come into collision on the top of a.. steps with those coming from the pit and zallcry. On the date of his visit this was the only means of ingress and egress. He fottod a flight of 15 steps about 4ft. wide, with two imitation doors at the bottom, each 23 inches wide, with an upright in the middle, leading from the upper boxes into a passage known as ‘• James' Wint," 6ft. Sin. wide. Both of these doors were securely nailed up and not at all available, and if they had been open the steps were much too steep for public use at such places in Cone of panic or fire. On the far side of the gallery and pit he dhcovered what had sometime been in-

PRIDE OF EATILESTOWN. RITENTLII TFMPLIL—An enters tainment in cnnnection with this Good Templar organisation was held on Wednesday evening In the Templars' Hell,. Bridge-strtet. 'rbere was a good a•tendance, and Brother E. Newman (saperintendot) presided. An excellent pro- ' gramme of songs. readings, arid recitation, w gone through.

• tended to use as doors opening into the back yard of the Derby Arms, but both were so securely fastened up that they could not be onenoi, and were covered with some kind of canvas which would prevent them being seen by ordinary observers ; and on examining the one outside leading from the pit he found it securely fastened up with a wooden bar screwed across it. This door opens into a passage only three feet wide. On examining the inside of the building he found one of the pillars supporting the boxes decayed at the bottom, and did not reach the ground within ten inches, and was spliced by a piece of thin board. Other pillars had sunk some six inches through be bad no dub', decay at the bottom, in his opinion rendering it an. safe in the event of a crowded house; and he felt convinced that this buildiug was unsuitable to be licensed as a theatre. It was altogether too much hemmed in by other buildings to allow sufficient means of egress, and if a panic through fire er other causes had arisen during the past year be feared the consequences would have been very serious, and he I trusted their worships would hesitate under the present cir- cumstances before ointinuing the license to a building which was so dangerous to the public, and which if crowded would contain over 1,000 persons. Supetintendent Leah added that he again visited the Theatre on Saturday morning. The pillar that did not touch the ground had been replaced, and the various doors which were securely fastened had been made available.

Mr. Fletcher said the report of Superintendent Leah had taken him very much by surprise. He did not anticibite until he came to that room that there was going to be any opposition on the part of the police. To discontinue the licence at once would subject Mrs. James to inconvenience and pecuniary lose, and he respectfully eubmitted it would hardly be in accordance with justice. Of course, the pubic must to protected, and it would not be right for the Bench to grant a licence fora building about which there was evert a doubt, so that he thought the proper course would be to licence the theatre for three months, and in the meantime the suggestions made by Superintendent Leah could have attention, a Arl the owner could see that the building was put in proper condition. So far as the building being' hemmed in was concerned, it was a condition of things which had exited Aloe the erection of the theatre, so that no alteration could be made. They could, however, improve the meats of ingress and egress, and he had evidence in court to show that the means were adequate when properly adapted. . .

The magistrates, after a long consultation in private, re- fused to grant the license. After such a report from the Superitteuden,, they did not think it would be in the int r- ests of the public to grant a licence to a building in that state.
Mr. Fletcher said this was a very serious business, and asked that the matter might be adjourned for a month, and in the meantime the detects would be remedied. • _ _

Mr. Brundrit said they could not a-dTo;t:n—it-.. They must either grant the licence or refase it, and they refused it, they thought, on very good grounds. Mrs. James could apply for a new licence at a future period, and it w ,uld be for the magistrates then on the Bench to say whether it would be entertained or not.

SHOCKING CRUELTY TO HORSES AT WIDNES. hieesrs. H. S. Hall, F. H. Goesage, and J. Brock were en- gaged at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, investia- ting sevenal cases of cruelty to horses.—Henry Bower, pe k butcher, Victoria-road, Widnes, was the first defendant, aid evidence was given by Inspector Ward and P.S. McGregor that about half-past eleven on the 18:h inst. Bower was driving a brown horse of which he is the owner along I Victoria-road. He drew up at the court-room door and the animal was examined. On the rear shoulder was a raw wound aboat the size of a florin, which must have caused ( ' the horee great pain. Behind the foreleg and underneath Ithe girth-strap was another wound of a painful nature. The animal was in low condition fled very lame. The defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. Hall said the defendant ought to be sent to p ieno, bet the Batch had decided that he must pay a fine of £2 and costs, with the alternative of a ,month a hard labour --Samuel Greenough, a driver, in the em- ploy of Messrs. cammick and Co., mineral water manufac- turers, St. Helens, was then charged with cruelty ti a berme by working it in an nu& state. Evidence was given by P.C. Lamb, P.S. McGregor and Police Clerk Steele. On the 17th inst. at noon the defendant was driving a team of I horses attached to a spring lurry through the town, and I Conatable Lamb observed that one of the animals was "un- easy." Underneath the collar was found a large raw wound, and on the breast NVVA another upwards of 2 inches lin length. Both wounds were of old standing, and the ham was In great pain.—The defendant alleged that there I was nothing wrong with the hot se when he started from Si. I Helens in the morning, and he called Mr. W. G. Dixon. I veterinary surgeon, who deposed that be was sent for to ex- amine a horse at Messrs. Camtnicks. The animal had a j wound shoat the s'ze of 61 on the 'if side. in , his opinion caused through the bursting of a I heat lump whilst out that day. He did not notice a wound ;on the breast. There was only a little hair rubbed off. In ' rep'y te Mr. Gossage witness said he could not say it was i the same horse that had been to Widnes. It was a grey I animal.—A boy was then called, and wee cross-questioned ,by Superiateodent Barker. He said his m,eter had two i grey horse", and admitted that be "ad told P.S. McGregor i that the hors- had been off work for a week on account of a I sore shoulder, and that he had been all over St. Helens on I the morning of the day in question in order to get another I horse to take its place.—The Bench imposed a rine of £2 and costs 16sa-- —Michael Doran, carter, of Milton-road, I • , Wadnee, was summoned on a similar charge —lnspector i Greenlee% R.S.P.O A ,deposed that an the 13th inst the de- fendant had his horse attached to a cart laden with ballast, lin the yard of the Widnes Alkali Comp tny's works. The I animal was old and in poor condition, and had three wounds on the off side of its back, which were discharging matter, ' and on the near aide WM a festering wound about the size I lof a crown piece. Thera vans el ,th underneath the saddle, ! setwated with matter from a raw wound.—P.S. Sttickland coroberced, atal the defendant was fined £1 and costs 13s.

Greening. A DISORDERLY IRISHELN. John Cunningham, a powerful looking Irishman, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on Friday morning; and he was also charged with assaulting Constable Baxen- dale and Joseph Owen, who assisted the constable. From the evidence it appeared that the prisoner had been ex- tremely violent. lie was sent to gaol for a month. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair, Alderman Pickmere, Councillor Greening, and Mr. . .

John Fair clough. Mismaxansors.—The following cases of drunkenness were dealt with as under :—Thomas Wilson, in Irlam- street, on Saturday evening, dismissed with a caution ; Jane Gill, in White- street, on Sunday morning, dismissed OR promising to leave the town ; Ann Bond, in the Market- place, on Saturday, also dismissed with a caution ;John ideCaffery, ira. Buttermarket-street, on Sunday evening, fined 50 and costs ; bridget Dolly, in Bewsey-street, ordered to pay costa; Ryan ildoDonehne, in Bridge-street, fined 5s and costs.--Eliz vbeth Ann Forster was charged with beg- ging in Knutsforrt-road.—P.C. Johnston said that she was in Knutsford-road, singing out of the Salvation Army War Cry, and he heard her beg at shops.—The Bench sent her to prison for 14 day.--Two men, named Carr and Ku. cannon, were charged with beinvirunk and disorderly and with fighting together in Fennel-street on Sunday afternoon. —They were each tined 5e and costs, or 7 days' imprison- inent.—Edward Toole, for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and omnibus in Bridge-street, on Saturday, was fined 2,6 d and costs.--Edward Uriffin, for disturbing the peace by fighting iu Winwick-street, was ordered to find a surety in £lO for his good behaviour, and be bound ever himself. igESDAY.—Before Councillor Greening and Mr. E. Jones, an inkeeper at Moore, as charged with bavivg assaulted an elderly man named Samuel Woods on the 17th inst.—Complainant stated that on the day in question he went into defendant's house to have a glass of porter, and haying entered into a dispute with a man about some ducks, defendant cel,ed him names and then run at him.—Evidence for the defence, however, showed that complainant had been using some very foul language, and that the defendant had only tapped him on tbe hat and threatened le put him out.—The case was dis- missed.
