div.head: .A STRANGE GHOST STORY.
div.p: .A STRANGE GHOST STORY.

EXTRAORDINARY PROCEEDINGS. A great sensation, and one that bee occasioned very lively comment, has arisen in St. Helens during the past few weeks by the alleged haunting of the manufactory of the world-famed pills of Messrs. Beecham. To say the least, the incidents which have occurred therein have been Of the most startling ciiaracter, and their exceedingly mys- terious nature has given rise to rumours that they are of supernatural origin. Whatever doubts may exist as to the latter theory, the occurrences are still unex: plained, and the mystery still remains unsolved. Messrs. Beecham's establishment is situated in Westfield-street, St. Helens, but some months ago they decided to rebuild.it on a more extended scale. In order to carry out these opera- tions the machinery was removed to another building In Lowe-street, belonging to the firm. The greater portion of this building was formerly used as a saw mill, but it remained unoccupied br a year or two. At present Messrs. Beecham oc- cupy the basement, comprising three rooms, while another portion of the ground floor is taken up by the ;Sr. Helena Industrial Co-operative Society, and the upper room is used as a barracks by the Salvation Army. Each dav the employes of Messrs. Beecham perform their accustomed duties without hindrance or inconvenience, but after darkness has set in for some two or three months past there have been nightly occurrences, which have given rise to every iinagiisable rumour as to" Ghosts and goblins.' Part of the duty of Mr. Andrews, the marager, has been to inspect the build- ing each night after the men bad left, and this has lately been an exciting and risky undeitaking. No sooner has Mr. Andrews entered the works to make his accustomed rounds than he has been assailed by an alarming ehower of stones, pieces of brick, copper slag, and other missiles, hurled with great force by some unseen hand. This has been an almost nightly occurrence for a considerable period, and the eluoi- dation of the mystery has baffled the most 'searching investigation of police officers and other inquirers. As an instance of the stone throwing, Mr. Andrews states that on Sunday night week he was in a little conservatory at the rear of the building with his son, about fifteen years I of age, and started to go his nightly roma% through the 'building. He opened the tuck door and he and his son walked in, when a missile, apparently launched at him, struck the door with great force. He looked round, but saw no one, as indeed he had seen no one on previous nights when he had experienced the same thing. He moved for- ward a little when another stone cattle in a slanting direc- tion and struck the wall. This was followed by another which struck some iron wheels, making a clear ring, and then the further door was struck by a Inertia. With toe view of unravelling the mystery, bands of workmen have been got together and atrolled the works and its neigh- bourhood, while the aid of the police has been sought. Scheme after scheme, however, for the detection of the author of the stone throwing has hitherto been unsuccess- ful. The steps taken to secure the stoppage of the unwel- come visitations have apparently been of a most coda- plet, character. For four successi^e nights, from sunset till daybreak, Mr. Andrews, with a staff of men, has paraded the works, but after the closest seerches they have failed to bring the mysterious individual to light. On another occasion five police officers entered the works and determined dot to leave the premises until they had captured the intruder. For that purpose the gas was left burning low, and the instant the stone throwing com- menced the lights were turned up, and this searchers rubbed In the direction from which the missiles had apparently proceeded, bat again the 'each was fruitless, and the policemen left the premises disappointed. On the night in question about 30 missiles, including pieces of bricks, stones, &e., were thrown, their weight averaging from four to five ounces. A suggestion was made that the mischief maker might be a member of the monkey tribe, but dogs were introduced without success, though the stones flew about as usual. Information as to these alarming pro- ceedings naturally spread throughout the town, and each I evening during the past fortnight the neighbourhood of Beecham's pill works has had an animated appearance: A crowd of some hundreds of persons have nightly gathered in the vicinity. The police have bad some difficulty in keeping the footpaths clear. The superstitious gossip- mongers in the vicinity have imagined all sorts of things, and rumours of 'ghosts and goblins" having been seen float- ing about have been circulated on every band. It is needless to add that these and numberless other asser- tions are absolutely without foundation. The genuine manifestations have been confined to stone-throwing, and of these mysterious occurrences there can be no douat. A large number of individuals have volunteered to render assistance in ferreting out the "invisible one," and Mr. Andrews, in several instances, has permitted them to undergo the trying ordeal. He states, however, that one trial has been sufficient to test the nerves of the bravest amongst them, and they have manifested an anxious desire to escape to a place of safety with all possible speed. Another singu- lar part of the affair is the fact that notwithstanding all the stones that have been flying about, neither Mr. Andrews nor any of those who have witnessed the occurrences have ever been injured or even struck by any of the atones. There have, however, been some very narrow escapes, many of the stones having passed within a few inches of the bodies and faces of those present. The only damage to the property inside has been the " dingeing" of doors and other woodwork, while a brass machine also bears evidence of having been struck by a von.. So violent and accurate was the stone throwing a short time ago that it was deemed advisable for the safety of Mr. Andrews to erect a wooden partition opposite the main entrance, and this partition still remains. The excitement attending the affairseemed to reach a culminating point on Sunday evening when some thousands of persons visited the spot. The crush round the doors to look inside the works through crevices in the door was so great that the gate was burst open. From seven o'clock on Monday evening until two o'clock on Tuesday morning thousands of per- sons flocked to the neighbourhood, but the crowd was a great deal more orderly than on the preceding evening. On Monday night two policemen and six of Mr. Beecham's employee were stationed outeide the building, while Mr. Andrews was on duty inside, with the view of capturing the "spirit." Notwithstanding these precautions, however, when Mr. Andrews paraded the works a large Stone about half a pound in weight was violently thrown and struck the wall near to where he then was. This was the only missile thrown during the night. On Tuesday morning a member of tae Salva- tion Army volunteered to solve the mystery, not by physi- cal means, but he declared he would invoke divine aid, and since Monday night the stone throwing has ceased, Mr. An- drews expressing the opinion to our representative on Thursday that he thought the manifestations woula cease "for the present." He added that he did not think the oc- currences were due to any supernatural agency, but he thought it was a clever dodge on the part of some scheming individual. In their efforts to discover tbe latter, men had surrounded the works, been on the roof, and stood at every door, and yet the stone throwing had gone on. He observed that one constable who was rambling in the dark through the works in his endeavours to discover the marauder fell down an old saw" pit" and so damaged his clothing that the firm purchased new articles of clothing for him. The room of the Salvation Army had also been visited by the nocturnal wanderer, and on one occasion the drum and money-box were struck, sending a rattle " through the room. Up to 1 hursday evening the strange affair had not been explained, but so long as it remains in Its present state the excitement is not likely to diminish. ANOTHER VISIT. For the last two days hopes have been entertained by Mr. Beecham, Mr. Andrews, his employes and public gener- ally that the extraordinary performances in stone throwing had Ceased, and that the "ghost" had either vanished en- tirely or removed his quarters. About half-past seven o'clock on Thurseav night, however, Mr. Andrews and his son went into the works to fetch out their overcoats, as the evening was wet. All seernid quiet, and Mr. Andrewn remarked that be should very muth like to do a little of the work which was in arrears owing to the dieturbancee, but that he was almost afraid to stay. He had scarcely uttered the words when a large piece of ceeper slag weighing half a pound came whizzing through the air, rolled over a number of parcels, struck a bench, and then dropped to the floor. Neither Mr. Andrews nor his son was hurt. Previous sus- picions have been carried into another channel by the following letter, which was on Thursday received by Mr. Beecham :—" Dear air,—ln reference to the ghost in Lowe-st by Reports i Sna von cannott find anything, have you, sir. Examined the floor, it is my firm °opinion Out there are someone Carrying on an illegal Business and that there are subturanean vault, of which you are not aware, it may be a subturanean Passage from (...towley Hill (C.M.) Perhaps dynamitards it is advisable to be very Cautious in the Proceeding er the consequences might be fatal should you fall on them in their lair they would in all probability be desperate it is qtsite evident there are someone there that have no business there, and you are a stumbling block in their way, and so they have formed a conspiracy to try to frighten you from the premises.' The envelope bears the Prescot postmark, and is directed to "Mr. Bore- ham, pil manufacturer; St. Helene (private.") The letter bears a signature, but until inquiries have been made it is not considered advisable to publish it. Mr. Andrews Says mans, persons have an idea that "Beech sin's Ghoet ' has bees " got rip" as an advertisement. but be states that no such idea has been entertained, and that the members of the firm are all mystified as to the extraordinery oocurrencee.

A young lady who was with them, the daughter of Mr. Pounder, boathuilder, wa% fortunately rescued. The deceased are the son and nephew of Mr. Geipel, shipowner, Hartlepool. "

, FROCKING FATALITY.—A shockine faCality was reported totbe Leicestershire coroner on Wednesday. It appears that a porter named Jobs Skinner was standing near the signals at Loseby station, watching a train from Leicester, wheal an express going I. Leicester came up unobserved and killed Skinner on the spot, his body being terribly mull. fated. The body was removed to Loseby to await an in- quest.

THREE LIVES LOST.— On Sunday a lire occurred at a house in Shoreditch, London, by which John Pearson, aged 50; Mary A. Walsh, aged 11; and Lydia H. Walsh, aged 4 years, lost their lives. It is supposed the tire was caci.ed by Pearson having tried to relight a paritfin lamp after it bad been extinguished.

• Ts PRINCH-OF WALBS nf IfORWAIr.-.-The Royal yacht Osborne, with the Prince ef Wales on board, arrived in the Skudeenaes Fjord on Sunday, and proceeded up the Hardanger Fjord to Odde, where she arrived at nine p.m. The Prince on Monday went on an excursion to the Sand- yen Lake in order to witness some net fishing. TOUPHDO BOATS —Arrangements are to be made at Chatham Dockyard for the storage of a larger class of tor- pedo boats than those hitherto constructed. it 'etingi in- tended to build some of the torpedo vessels of a much greater length and coinage than those being constructed. The new class of torpedo boats will be ab.ut 200 feet in length. SHOOTING A BAHMAID.—Bobert Hay, aged 60, landlord of the Barley Mow lan, Colchester, has attempted to murder his barmaid, Alice Ashington. Hay is a widower and re- sided alone with the barmaid. They had a qu Arrel, Hay being the worse for liquor, and he fired a revolver three times, the last shot entering her head. She now lies in a erificai condition. Jealou.y is supposed to be the cause of the crime .

Ssunios RLILWAT COLLTSION.—A. eoUieon occnrred ow the District Railway near Earl's Court Station, Londoa, en Sunday afternoon. A Great-Western train ran into a dis- trict train as both trains were going slow. The driver of tho former was so seriously crushed that he died not long afterwards, and the stoker and a paseenger were seriously injured. A failure in the connecting rod of the signal was the cause of the accident.

EXTRAORDINARY SUICIDE —A boy, named Sermon, aged 12, has been drowned in Birmingham under extraordinary circumstances. His mother had been trying to get him sent to Canada, and this preyed on his mind, and, while standing on the side of the canal, he said, "They are going to send me to Canada. and I would rather drown myself than go." He immediately jumped into the water, was sucked into the lock-nit, and wax drowned.

These are;the converts whO were reported a few weeks ago in some quarters to brave been kilbd. COTTON MILL FIRE NEAR ROCHDALE —On Sunday 'Mews. Littlewoods, to- gether with the Rochdale Corporation's steam engine and hoee carriage. succeeded in confining the Aimee to that part of the building where the fire originated. The damages are estimated at snout £3 000, which is cevered by insurance. THE 400nt ANNIVERSARY OF BOSWORTH FIELD.— Although Saturday was the 409th anniversary of the hattle of Bosworth, the event was not marked by any celebrations in the district. A few visitors went over tber famous field, and on Saturday, and Sunday considerable numbers visited the :mime of King Richard the Third's departure from Leices- ter, be having slept) at the Blue Bur Inn, still th a site of an hotel, the night before the battle. Tne memorial stone wbich marks the resting place of the last of the Plantagen- ets aleo excited considerable,attention. LORD HARTINGTON AT ILELEY.—Speaking at a Church bazaar at Ilkly, on Wednesday. the Marquis of Hartingten said there might have been times when toe Church of Eng- land hid displayed some apathy and fallen stornewhat be- hind the highest conception of her duties, but now, stimu- lated by the healthy competition of other Churches and the energetic spirit of her leaders, there could be no doubt as to the value of the work she was doing in supplying in crowded cities and secluded parishes, if not the only influence, at any rate one of the most powerful influences which con- nected daily toil and drudgery with a higher life. THE IRISH PARLIAMENTARY PARIT.—On TtleSday, at private meeting in Dublin of the Irish Parliamentary Party, ander the presidency of Mr. Parnell. M.P., it was resolved that Parliamentary. candidates should be selected at county conventions acting in consultation with Mr. Parnell and his colleagues. It was further resolved that each candidate should sign A pledge to the effect that he would vote and act with the party, and resign if called on to do so by the majority of his colleaeues. Speaking at a public meeting held subsequently, Mr. Parnell said the triumph of the cause was assured whether the Whigs or the Tories won at the next election. The Tories would give them as good a scheme of self-government as the Whigs. The farmers should support the National League, and so show that they would not be trampled upon by the landlord during the en- suing winter. METHODISM IN GREAT BRITAIN AND IRELAND. Now that all the Conferences connected with Methodism in Great Britain and Ireland for the current year have been held, it will interest many to know the present numerical strength of the parent body and its various effehoots. The follow- ing figures give the exact returns of fully accredited church- members. Besides these, there are meeting in classes as members on trial and members in junior society classes, fully one hundred thousand more, who will be forthcoming during the year :—Weeleyan Methodists, 413,263, increase, 2,797 ; Primitive Methodists, 192,389, inc-ease, 1,281 ; United Methodist Free Churches, 76,385, increase, 544 ; Methodist New Connexion, 29,327, decrease, 60; Bible Christians, 26,359, increase, 314 ; W'eelevanta in Ireland, 24917, increase, 105. Total membership, 762,594; increase 5,041. Mg. Bray, M.P AND TRADE DEPRESSION.—The Lan- (natl.:re, Cheshire, and Staffordshire Federation of Miners held a demonstration at Burslem, on Slenday. The speakers were Mr. Burt, M.P., who said they were at present passing through A period of extreme trade depresaion. Perhaps trade depression was not the proper term to apply, because if they looked at facts and statistics they found that during the last ten years, comprising, that was to say. 1883 and 1884 with 1873 and 1874. the produce of coal had increased LO an extent of not less than 31 millions of tons ; so that in reality it was over-production. It was bee tilde there was such an immense reserve power of production that imme- diately there was any tendency to improve wages and priors, surplus produce came is to keep wages and prices down at a low level. He sympathised with every honest and well- directed effort on the part of the working pspulation to im- prove their condition. He wanted working men te have better wages, better house accommodation and more leisure. A Dnetterriost OP LIBERALISM--In a letter to the Pall Mall Gazette, Professor J. S. Blackie says :—I was much amused the other day by some curious correspondence in your columns from a reverend gentleman seeking the true defini- tion of the creed of Liberalism. Definitions in politics, as in religion, are more curious than useful; nevertheless there is no harm in making them occasionally, as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews has done in a well-known place (Het). xi., 1). The answer of his Grace of Argyll to the question, "What is Liberalism ?" was, as usual with him, full of wisdom and point; hut as definitions ought to be short, I will give you one which I hope may appear satisfac- tory in a single sentence. Liberalism is that tendency in the minds of politicians which inclines them to grant as much freedom and scope to individual self.assertion in the members of a social bady as is consistent with the general good of the whole ; while C mservatism, as an antagonistic force, is that tendency in the minis ef politicians which leads them to preserve as far as posaible intact the rights and privileges, functions, and interests of the governing classes as they have been hancl,d down to the present by the institutions, laws, and consuetudes of the past. The watchwords of the one piety, accordingly, are liberty and progress; of the other, authority and stability •, and in the balance of thess two antagonistic forces, according to time, place, and circumstances, good government consists. DEMONSTRATION IN HYDE PARK —A great demonstra- tion took place in Hyde Park on Saturday afternoon in sup- port of the movement for the protection of girls, from forty to fifty thousand persons being estimated to be present. Several contingent*, each with bands and banners, marched from various districts of London, these including the Church Army in full regalia, the Women's Trade Union. the National Repeal Aasociation, the Women's Suffrage As- sociation, the Young Men's Christian Association, and the London Trades Associations. Deputations from Edinburgh, Leeds, Sheffield, Kettering, Bristol, and other towns joined in the central procession, which started from the Thames Embankment, and banners draped with black were 'carried. Eleven platforms were erected in the park by the promoters of the movement, but in addition to these there were inds-' pendent platforms for the friends of the Socialist League and Social Democratic Federation. There was an immense gathering of spectators in additima to those who took active part in the proceedings. and although there were several ugly rushes, comparatively good order was maintained. Sir. Wm, McArthur, M.P., who was one of the principal speakers, urged a vigorous enforcement of the new Act until crimes such as those which had lately horrified the country were extirpated. Mr. Broadhurst. M.P., expressed the opinion that the evil arose from the fact that men were driven into tt-e towns from healthy districts, and became herded in small habitations, the result being low wages, vice, and immorality. Mr. Michael Devitt, whe was greeted with loud cheeritig. attributed the evil to the present stire of the land laws, which he said were vic- ious in the extreme, and must be reformed. The people were suffering from an idle and a good.formothing AI ie.. tocracy ani they mus• be saved from the bereJitary plun- derer. An ichn•ic resolution calling upon the public to as- sist the authorities in the vigorous enforcement of the Act was carried, amid cheers, at the Various platforms, and the crowd dispersed quietly.

The following correspondence respecting the miners' pro- gramme has passed between Mr. Samuel Woods, miners' agent, Bryn, and Colonel McCerquodalo, J.P , D.L., the Liberal candidate for the Newton Division of South-west Lancashire :
A telegram from Madrid states that a popular morement is being organised in favour of granting Certain tariff con- cessions to England.

A distress to recover extraordinary tithes took place at Lower 11.1ston, Kent, on Friday. The farmers passed reso- lutions condemning tithes. Official inquiry at Sr. Petersburg has elicited the fact that the recent robbery of 220 000 roubles from the State Bank was committed by employee of the bank. A steam boiler on the premises ef Mr. R. Prestwich, hat- box maker, Guide Bridge, exploded on Thursday afternoon, causing the death of a youth named John Prestwich, nephew of the owner, who was himself injured. At the Gravesend police court, on Wednesday, Martha Eliza Bushy and Mary Church Underwood, charged with wilfully setting fire to premises, in which usederwood resi- ded as companion to Busby, were committed for trial. A Reuter's Bergen telegram reports that the Sunbeam arrived at Veblungsnas on Thursday. The weather was cold and wet, and the mountains were covered with snow. Mr. Gladstone drove to Ramsdalen, and will next go to Molds.

There was a conflict on Thursday between police and people at Mullinavatt, connty Kilkenny, on an attempt being made to evict some tenant farmers. Batons, bayonets, an stones arc said to have been used, to the serious discom- fort et both parties.

Bombardier Mitchell, Royal Marine Artillery, was sen- tenced by naval court martial at Portsmouth, on Wednes- day, to three months' imprisonment for having, when acting as postman to the gnardship Hector, stolen certain parcels, letters, and bills committed to his care.

The steamer Queen, when making the entrance of the Tees late on Wednesday night, met a steam launch, near North Gare Breakwater, in distress. The Queen had barely time to rescue one of the three occupants when the lauoch went to pieces. Her owner and master were drowned.

PROPOSED PURCHASE OE WATERWORIS.—The Northwich Local Board have obtained sanction for a loan of £40,000 to purchase the undertaking of the Northwich Waterworks Company, and to carry out works of water supply, dm, for the district. Mr. Win. Robert Stow, A Frome has been appointed the surveyor to the Board, out of 60 applicants for the office.

Reimer ACCIDENTS.—A report upon the number of railway accidents in .the United Kingdom, published by the Board of Trade, shows that 1,135 persons were killed and 4,100 were injured during the year in the working of the railways. The proportion of passengers killed during the year is returned as one in 5,/48,083, and the proportion in- jured as one in 466024. SAD ACCIDENT.—EarIy on Thursday morning Mr. John Rostrup, ship chandler, whilst crossing a gangway connect- ing the ship Wyoming with the side of a Liverpool dock, and having in his arms the infant child of Captain Ander- son, slipped and fell into the dock. He and the infant were soon got out, but they bad received such injuries that both died cool afterwards.

ATTEMPTED MURDER or A BARMAID.—Robert say, a publican, aged 60, was charged before the Colchester magis- trates on Thureday with shooting Alice Ashenton, a bar- maid, on Tuesday, with intent to murder her. The prose- cuting solicitor said the injured woman was in Colchester Hospital: and, although progressing satisfactorily, a period of quiet and rest was enjoined, and she could not appear. The accused was remanded for a week.

TO COLOIIBL MCCORQUODALB. Dear sir,—Some of our Tory friends not being satisfied with the personal exposition of your views on " our miners' parliamentary programme " which you were good enough to give to me and the deputation that waited upon you in April last, and as letters have appeared in a local paper ask- lug for your views more in detail, I shall be glad if you will please oblige me with a reply for publication.—Yours truly (Signed) S. Woorm. Gadlys, Menai Bridge, Anglesey, August 19th, 1835. TO MR. Sh WOODS. My Dear Sir.—On account of being from borne on impor- tant business, my reply is somewhat delayed. Agreeably, however, to your request. I now have the pleasure of send- ing you my answers to the questions you sent me some time ago.—Yours faithfully (Signed) GBO. MCCOED:DIODALB. MINERS' PARLIAMENTARY PROGRAMME.—QUES- TIONS AND ANSWERS. I. Will you vote for the bill to amend the Employers' Liability Act of 1880, as introduced by Mr. Burr, M.P. ? I would be prepared to vote for amending the Employers' Liability Act. 11. Will you vote for the necessary amendments to Mines Regulation Act—via. (a) That miners may select their checkweighmen from any place (tile same right the em- ployers have at the present time) ;: (b) That miners may have the right to prosecute without being forced to get the Home Secretary's sanction, as at present (the same right the employers possess now) ?—Yes ; employers and em- ployed should be placed on the same platform. 111. Will you vote for a thorough reform of the Land Laws 2—Yes.

IV. Will you vote for a Royal Commission to be ap- pointed for inquiry into Royalty Acts ?-I.,would not object to this. It mar be productive of benefit, and, tio doubt, useful information for the benefit of the nation may he ob- tained.

BOILER EXPLOSION AT GUIDE BRIDGE.—At DOOR on Thursday a boiler explosion took place at the Hat Box Works of Richard Houghton Prestwich, Guide Bridge, de- molishing part of the kuilding.. A lad named John Peter Prestwich, who was in the boiler house, was fearfully scalded. Mr. Prestwich, who is a member of the Auden- shaw Local Board, was in his office with another mentber of the board, Johe Hamm, a retired gentlemen. Both were badly scalded, and the office was wrecked. BIRMINGHAM MUSICAL FaxrivaL.—Gounod's new oratorio " More et Vita " was performed for the first time at the Bir- mingham Musical Festival on Wednesday, arid was well re- ceived. It was admirably rendered by the principals, chorus, and orchestra. In the first part, which was the portion given on Wednesday, the principal solos are allotted to soprano and tenor, and these were sung by Madame Albani and Mr. Edward Lloyd. The evening concert had for its chief item the pleasing cantata " Yule Tid:' by Mr. Thos. Anderson, of Birmingham.

BRADLAUGEI AT NORTITAMPTON.—Mr. Bradlaugh, in his address to the Northampton electors, issued on Wednes- day, says every Liberal candidate, almost without excep- tion, is &elating in favour of Northampton's constitutional rights. The electors of East Finsbury had nominated him as a protest candidate, and had promised to elect him to vindicate their electoral rights, but it is the return of the Northampton electors which be desired to carry to the table. He asked them to do as Middlesex did for John Wilkes renew his credentials to the new Parliament
V. win you vote for abolition of the London Coal Dues ? —Yes.

TILE WELSH EISTEDDFOD.—Sir G. Elliott, M.P., delivered the presidential address at the National Eisteddfod of Wales, at Aberdare, on Tuesday, at which Lord Aberdare and Mr. Matthew Arnold were also present. Previously Sir George was presented with a congratulatory address by a body of workmen. The proceedings at the National Eisteddfod at Aberdare terminated on Tuesdty, and Wednesday's pro- gramme commenced with a meeting of the Cymmrodorion Society, at which a paper was read by Mrs. Bryant on uni- versity local examinations in Wales. The Eisteddfod meet- ing was afterwards entered upon. THE RECALL OP SIR CHARLES WARREN..—ThE Daily News understands that Sir Charles Warren, her Majesty's Special Commissioner in Bechuanaland, has been recalled by the Secretary of State for the Colonies. We have reason to believe that it is not owing to any representation made to her Majesty's G-overnrnent by the Cape Ministry that Sir Charles Warren hag been recalled They have neither directly nor indirectly taken any part in the matter. Col. Stanley. acting in concert with Sir Heronles Robinson, is responsible for the supercession of her Majesty's Special Commissioner. We are informed that Sir C.. Warren will return to England immediately.

A CHILD DROWNED 2L'l' LOWTON.—On Thursday after- noon, Mr. W. T. Hust.aud, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Hare and Hounds public•heuse, Lowton, touching the death of Alice Tongs two years and nine months old, daughter of Wilbraham Tongs, an inspector ot nuisances for the Leigh Union, and residing in Church-lane, Lowton. Near Mr. Tonge's house is a small pond, which that gentle- man railed in some time ago. On Monday afternoon, while Mr. and Mrs. Tonge were having tea, they missed their child. A few minutes later the body et the child was found floating in the pond, face downwards. Be is supposed that the deceased crept beneath a small gate in the railings and while playing near the water fell in and' was drowned. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned."

VI. Will you vote for free education would vote for amending the present Act, taking care to avoid changes calculated to interfere with the present religious teaching, being anxious to maintain the present excellent manage- ment of our denominational schools, which are working ex- ceedingly well in this district. I would urge the substitu- tion of the School Attendance Committees for that of Boards of litardians to decide when school fees should not be re- quired from poor parents. VII. Will you vote for payment of members of Parlia- ment 13—Believing that the present representatives of the working classes have rendered good service, I consider that moderate remuneration, or payment, might be sanctioned for a limited number of members, seeing that their occupation prevents their having the necessary means, and that their .services would be advantageous to the State.
VIII. IVill you vote for the bill empowering rate- payers to paw returning officers' fees under certain speci- fied conditions, as introduced by Mr. Broadhurst, 111.1'1— Yes.
IX. Will you vote for a thorough reform of the House of Lords ?—Yes. .

It is estimated that about tbree•fifths of the voting power of the Newton Division is now vested in the miners, who are taking a lively interest in their " programine." Tke main body of the men are, it is stated, dissatisfied with the published reply to the above questions fro n Sir Richard Cross, M.P., the Tory candidate, and it is believed Colonel McCorquodale's favourable decision respecting the various questions will do much to ensure his return.

MEETING Ar BILLINGE. A !MSS meeting of miners was held in the open air at Billinge. on Tuesday night, when NIT% S. Woods, miners' agent, of Bryn, lectured on "Sir Richard Cross's Answer to the Miners' Programme." Mr. Paul Hall (Earlestewn) pre- sided, and there WAS a large aed attentive audience.. The CHAIRMAN said the subject of the lecture was especially interesting to the miners. It was very important that they should understand what Sir Richard Cross's views on these questions were. The reply had been published, and he (the speaker) believed that when the miners read it they would come to the conclusion that Sir Richard Cie:tee would not be a suitable man to represent them in the House of Commons. Colonel MeCorquodale'e replies had now been published, from which they would see that he was very favourable to their programme. He was the most likely to protect their interests, and he (the chairman) be- Keyed the miners of the Newton Division would do their duty at the general election, and return Col. McCorquodale by an overwhelming majority. (Applause.) Mr. WOODS congratulated his hearers on at last having been recognised as citizens of the most important empire in the world—a right which had been given to theme, by Atf. Gladstone's Franchise Bill. He said he had put the miners' programme before Colonel McCorquodale and Sir R. Cross, not as a Liberal or a Conservative, but as the re- presentative of working-men. Colonel McCorquodale- had. practically pledged himself to support the whole of the questions, which he was good enough to say were only fair and reasonable, Sir Richard Crosa'S replies, as published in the pepere, were very disappointing and discouraging to them as miners. He was not prepared te go in for the amendment of the Employers' Liability Act, which he con- sidered was a liberal measure. As to the Mines Regulation Act, Sir It. Cross said he was not aware of any hardships respecting miners' checkweighmen and VI question of pro- secution of employers. As a lawyer, Sir R. Cross must have seen the numerous cases brought before the courts in which the injustice to miners had been made known.. Mas- ters could object to any weiglernan employed by the men, and in cases of alleged fraud the miners were oledged to ob- tain the Home Secretary's sanction before they could prose- cute—a barrier which took up much time, and WAS a hard- ship the employers were not called upun to endure.. As to the land question, Sir Richard Cross seemed to regardiit as one which did not affect the miners. Sir R. Cross was-op- posed to paying members of Parliament, but be wae not opposed to receive £5,000 a year as Home Secretary, and yet his salary had to be paid by. the taxpayer. Colonel McCorquodale was in favour of a limited number of paid members, and he recognised that woreingnaen's representatives had rendered good service to the State. Col. McCorquodale was prepared to vote for a thorough reform of the Hones of Lords; but Sir It. Cross had practically said "No" to every question. He (the speaker) urged the men to go in for a man who would improve their pecitiun and that of their families. (Applause.) The following reaolation was. submitted :—" That this meeting considers Col. McCorquodale a fit and proper person to represeet the Newton Division in the House oft Com- mons, and pledges itself to use all legitimate means to secure his return." The motion was carried with anslama- tion, as Was also a resolution thanking Mr. Gladstenele Government for passing the Ftanchise Bill. A hearty vote of thanks accorded to the chairman and Mr.. Woods terminated the proceedings.

THH MIIRDNR IN BLENIIHIM P.a.—George Boddington, the man in custody on the charge of murdering William Beckley in Blenheim Park on the 12th inst., was brought before Mr. Barnett and the Hon. E. Ponsombg at the Wood- stock Town Hall on Thursday morning Ku remand. The remaining evidence to complete the case was that of Mr. Fisher. the public analyst for tho county of Oxford, who stated that he had examined the grubbing axe with which the prisoner had confessed he committed the deed, but had failed to 6nd blood stains Either on the handle or the blade. On the right sleeve of the prisoner's shirt he found several small blood stains on the inside and one near the wrist, but could not say that it was human blood. He had examined a epade and the prisoner's clothing, but had failed to find am, traces of blood except on the inside of one of the pockets of the coat, where there were marks as if a rabbit or some other animal had been put there—The prisoner, being cautioned in the usual way, said be bad nothing to say, and be was committed to take his trial at the Oxford Assizek

WORK AND WAGES —The collections in the mills of Blackburn, on Saturday. in aid of the weavers' strike at Chorley amounted to £34 125.—A meeting of minders con- nected with the Oldham strike is about to be held on Satur- day, when the question of considering a compromise will be dealt with.—An Attempt was made on Tuesday to bring the miners' strike at Ilkeston to an end. The men offered to resume work at a reduction of ens penny per ton. The masters offered to lower their demand to twopence per ton. This the men refused to Sc. cept, and the strike therefore still continues, much distress prevailing in the district. The mill- spinners and manufacturers of Dundee have re- solved to still further reduce wages after the 4th of September, to the extent of 5 per cent —A meeting of dele- gates of the Bolton and District Cotton Operatives' Asso, dation, numbering 400, and representing 4 000 members was held in Dolton, on Wednesday night, to consider a re- solution of the masters to reduce the wages of operatives five per cent. The lengthened period of depression in trade —caused mainly by over-production—has been severely felt, and various methoeim have been adopted to meet it. There was a very animated discussion at the meeting, and it was resolved to adjourn the decision for a meeting of re- presentatives in Manchester, the decision to be taken next Wednesday night. LORD RIPON AT BOLTON —A great Liberal meeting was held ou Monday night in the Temperance Hall at Bolton, for the purpose of hearing an address from the Marquis of Ripon. Mr. James Bodow, president of the local Liberal Association, occupied the chair. A motion returning thanks to Lord It pun for his presence and express- ing emphatic approval of his policy as Viceroy of India was proposed by Mr. Robert Leake, M.P , seconded by Mr R. N. Philips, M.P., and enthusias- tically adopted. In his speech in reply, Lord Ripon dealt exclusively with Indian affairs. He described the position of the Afghan question at the time of his appoin•ment to tho Viceroyalty, and explained a 9 he bad dune on several previous occasions that the object of the policy he inaugura- ted on his arrival in India wan to re-unite Afghanistan under one strong ruler, to maintain friendly relations with him, to be ready to aid him in holding Pishin, and to be ready to complete the railway to Quettah and the foot of the passes. He adopted that policy in provision of the events which had since occurred, and all those events had prily tended to confirm his belief ..that that policy was sound. Proceeding to defend his policy against the attack recently made upon it by Lord R. Churchill, he claimed that the reduction of the salt duta. in India gave substantial relief to the great bode of people, and that, further, he was enabled to carry out with a large reduction of taxation most valuable public Nvorks which would afford security against the worst evils of famine. He also claimed that he left the finances of India in a sound and healthy condition, wad therefore in the condition best calculated to enable the country to meet any sudden emergency. He was content to appeal (min Lord It. Churchill ti the t.eople of India, and he could well afford to accept without a murmer carping criticisms of party rheteric• He could do so all the more easily when he recalled to mind those great manifestations of loyalty to British rules which bad been displayed during the last few months.

EARLESTOWN. Tun Summed Buxom IFtneruem. or Tzta DECEASED. —The remains of the man Josepla,Webster, who killed him- self by lying in frost of. goods train at St. Helena Jaction, on Monday week, were interred in the burial ground at- tached to Sutton Church, on Friday afternoon; Early on the morning of thatiday the body had been removed from the Railway Hotel, St—Helene inaction where it had lain until after the inquest, and was enclosed a coffin, which bore the inscription, "ibseph Weboter, died August 17th, 1885, aged 58 years." It was conveyed te the house of his brother- in-law, John Woodcock, Diormaree-road. The coffin was placed in a shillebeer provided by Mr. J. W. Fowler, and about half a dozen relations attended. The body wee borne by seven or eight awn from the Sutton Rolling Mills, al which the deceased had been employed. When the corteje• had arrived at the churchyard the coffin was placed upon a bier and carried to the extreme oorner of the grounds, where it was depositediles a grave without any service of any kind. 'The relations were visibly affected, and threw earth upon the coffin. Some hundreds of persons viewed the procession as it passed through Sutton, but only about 50 persons assembled at the grave side. Mr....Ferrand, from the sidichors' department, Lime-street, prosecuted, and said•that appeared to. be one of the cases which bad occurred so fre- quently of late in which passengers took a ticket to Edge Hill, and then went a greater distance. Mr. Pedler, Mathew. master at Collins Green, having given. evidence; Frederick Shaw, a respectable looking young mao, was called,. He said he was in the company's service and was .employed at the Viaduct Works, Earlestown. lie, came by the seine train as the prisoner on tne previous afternoon from Liver- pool. When he entered the carriage there were two-young women in Vac compartment with her, but they afterwards lett, fie was smoking a pipe. and did not speak to Turner natil they got within about ni yards of Conine Green Station, when be told her what village it was. She inform,tl ' him that the booking clerk at Liverpool had etiven her ii ticket for Edge tiill in mistake, and in The hurry she kid not picked • up her change. She inouir..d if he won't] be good enough to explain this 10 ,the station-imaster, and tele him she asked for a ticket to Wkerington. He agreed to In so, but on getting out of the train she informed The station- (raver that she had first seen him at the Grapes Hotel, new Lime-street Station, that, afternoon ; that they had re- mained there a conetderable time, and on going to the station she at hie request gave him 29 with which to get her a ticket. On his saving there was not an atom of truth in this statement. she said he had also attempted to criminally asseult her in the carriage.—Prisoner (moaning, and very excitedly) : Oh, you bad man ?—ln defence, Turner did nor k allude to the assault, lout said she paid for a ticket to War- rington, where she was going to see her nephew, as work was S 0 bail to get at Bootle. She also maintained that she was with the last witness at the Grapes, and gave him the !b.—The Bench fined the woman 5s and Els costs, or in de- fault seven days. She moaned and-wept, and it was only with difficulty that the officers prevented her making a scene in the oeurt room.

OUR VOLUNTEERS AT ALDERSHOT. (Communicated.) A girl in a neighbouring city married a chimney sweep, because she felt he would soot her. - • •

" Why, Sam, how do you expect to get that mule along with a spur only on one side ?" "Well, boss, if I gets dat side to go, ain't de udder one boun' to keep up ?" Hs OUGHT TO KNOW.—" Where are my new pants ?" said a newly-married husband one morning to his wife. "Well, William, you ought to know best ; I think you wore them last," was the reply. NOT FASHIONABLH.—" Are checks fashionable now ?" asked a highly-dressed dude of his tailor as he looked over his goods. "I don't believe they are, air," was the reply, "for I haven't teen any around lately." He looked so hard at the young man when he said it that it caused an absence in the shop very rapidly. A Boston gentleman who had tarried too long at a wine- supper found his wife in a high state of nervonsnessawaiting his return. She said, "Here I've been waiting and rocking in a chair until my head swims round like a top !" "Jess so where I've been," responded he' "it's in the atmosphere." A MulacLE.—Pretty Teacher: Now, Johnny Wells, can you tell me what is meant by a miracle ?—Johnny: Yes, teacher, mother says if you don't marry the new parson it will be a miracle.—Teacher: You may sit down. Call a girl a chick, and she smiles; call a woman a hen, and she howls. Call a young woman a witch, and she is pleased; call an old woman a witch, and she is indignant. Call a girl a kitten, and she rather likes it; call a woman a cat, and she will hate you. Queer sex. It was at the breakfast table. Mr. Smilingboy was telling Mrs. S. about the performance of a farce he had attended the night before. "An," said he, "my dear, you'd have died laughing if you could have seen it!' Then he added. ha a tone of burning enthusiasm, "Flow I wish you'd teen there!" Even now he cannot understand why Mrs. S.'s remarks directly afterwards took such an nnuaually violent personal turn.

FEAUFUL WILD-Fora..—A Sunday-school teacher, reading the words "The fowls of the air" to her class, proceeded to aek them, "What are 'the fowls of the air'?" After a pause, one little girl solved the problem by replying " Please, miss, it's the bad smell;!"

A lad); with a fatal squint came once to a fashionable artist for her portrait. He looked at her and she at him, and both were embarrassed. He spoke first, "Would your ladyship permit me," he said, "to take the portrait in pro- file? There is a certain shyne,.a about one of your ladyship's eyes which is as difficult in art as it Is fascinating in nature.' He had his way. A woman who started to jump into the river and drown herself suddenly remembered that she had left the cat in the pantry, and hurried back home. She afterwards said, "The idea of my struggling in the water, and thinking that the cat was a-licking the cream off my milk in the pantry at that very minute was more than I could bear,"

"Oh, Lord!" he groaned, " rye swallowed it." " Well, for goodness sake," whispered the wife, "keep quiet, or you'll wake the baby."

- - - A Ituasas aciarNsx Rot/wt.—Arrangements were being made for an amateur representation of "Romeo and Juliet." Mrs. S. was cast for "Juliet," bat some difficulty was had in finding a suitable "Romeo." "Why don't you play Romeo yourself, Mr. S.?" suggested one of the young ladies. "You would do it splendidly, I am sure." " What ! ' he exclaimed," with Mrs. S. ' Juliet ?' Why, we've been married three years." "Have another piece of the cake," said Johnny's mother to a female friend who was taking tea with her. "No, don't do it," put in Johnny; "it will make you ill." "Why, Johnny, ain't you ashamed of yourself to talk in that way?" said his mother. 'Well, mother, that is what you always tell me when I want another piece' and I am sure I can eat four times as much as Mrs. Green can!" answered Johnny.

, SQUARING THE ClRcutt—The valet of a young Parisian exquisite carried, on behalf of his master, a splendid bouquet to a rich young widow, who exclaimed on seeing it, " Oh, What a lovely bouquet! But Jules, dear fellow' is quite too lavish with his money. I woader how much he gave for the flowers ?" "I beg your pardon," replied the servant ; "coy master has, so to speak, paid nothing for them, as everything is to be squared after you and he are married." Two Highlandmen, being in Glasgow for the first time, were having a walk through the city. Turning a corner, they were much surprised to see a water-cart wetting the street. Not having seen anything of the kind before, Tonga!, under a mistaken idea, ran after the cart and cried out to the driver, "Hey, man—hey man, you're losln' a' yer water !" His friend, annoyed at Tougal's want of knowledge, ran after him, caught him by the arm, and said rather testily, "Tougal, man Tonga!, don't be showin' your Ignorance; div you'll no see it's to keep the laddies aff the back o' the cairt ?" . . .

Tuts MOTRHR KNEW.—Fond mother: "Now look here, George! I want you to break off with that girl. She is very pretty and all tha• ; but I know her too well to want you to risk your life and happiness by marrying her. Why, she knows no more about housekeeping than I do about Greek—not a bit !" George : "Perhaps not ; but she can learn." Mother: "After marriage is rather late for that, George." George : "But you said yourself that you did not know a thing about housekeeping until after you were married." Mother : "Very true, George—and your poor father died of dyspepsia twenty years ago!" Tau lt HISTORY OF TllB PLANT.—St. DiClO77BlllB was 011 his way from his monastery on Mount Olympus to Naxos. and he sat down to rest during the heat of the day. Close to him he saw a pretty plant which he wished to take with him, and, lest it should wither by the way, he put it into the leg-bone of a bird, and to his surprise, at his next halt. lug place he found it had sprouted ; so accordingly he put it into the leg-bone of a lion, and the same thing occurred ; finally, he put it into the leg-bone of an ass, and, on reach- ing Naxos, he found the plant so rooted in the bones that he planted them all together; and up came the vine, from the fruit of which he made the first wine, a little of which made the saint sing like a bird, and a little more made him strong as a lion, and yet a little more made him foolish as an ass. BuYinG lits Owls Ftsu.—A youig City man who was trout-CAlng in the country followed a brook with no suc- cess until it passed under a fence Into a pasture. He climbed the fence, and, as he cast his fly at the root of a willow tree, he observed that a gaunt rustic was watching him. Finding however, that he made ho protest, the young man continued fishing, and presently he had seven fair trout in his basket. As he placed his foot on the lower rail of the fence to depart he was accosted by the countrymen, who said grimly, ")rap them trout !" The City man hesitated. " Drap 'em, or I'll drop you into the brook !" continued the countrymen. The young oxen then emptied the contents of his basket, and climbed the fence, saying as he reached the safe side, "Well, I have met mean men; but, for generous, whole-sonled mean- ness, you b,at them all !" " Hold on, young fellow ! " said the farmer. "I ain't mean. If I'd wanted to be mean, rd ha' stopped you fishin', or charged you a crown for the chance. Now, If you want to buy a nice string of fish you can hav'm for a florin—and I reckon they're aheap at the price." The young man paid the florin.
ELECTRIC HOUSE BELLS.
REPRFSENTATION OF TAILORS .IN PARLIARRIIT.—At a

----- conference in Glasgow, os Monday evening, of Atnalgamated Tailors of Great Britain and Ireland, it was unanimously agreed that the time had arrived when labour should be more adequately represented in Parliament. The conference therefore pledged themselves to use their utmost endeavours to raise all necessary expenses by voluntioy subscriptions amongst members for the purpose of returning one of their own trade to the Howe of Commons. It was carried that the next conference be held at Belfast. Mr. Bailey (Preston) was reappointed president, and Mr. Davy vice—president ; Means. Holly, Kier, McDade, and Goodman were added to the executive. _ _

----- -- • MR. PARNELL, M.P.. ON RIICRNT IRISH LEGISLATION.— Speaking at a banquet in Dublin, on Monday night. Mr. Parnell, M.P., said he only linked upon the Acts the legis- lative enactments which they ltad been enabled to wring from an unwilling Parliament as means towards an end that they would have at any time in the hour of their deepest depression and greatest discouragement, spurned and re- jected any measure, however tempting and however much apparently for the benefit of the Irish people, if they had been able to detect that behind it lurked any danger to the legislative independence of Ireland. (Cheers.) And although during this Parliament which bad now expired they might have said very little about Home Rule, very little about legislative independence, very little about Re- peal of the Union, yet from each of their hearts the thought of how these great things might be best forwarded was never for a moment absent. It was a marvel to him that Ireland had been so well served as it had been during the past five years. The present position of Ireland was ad- mitted by all parties to be that the question of legislative in- dependence was on the point of solution. (Cheers.) The question referred to is as follows :—" Will you vote against the hereditary principle in the House of Lords whenever it is proposed in the House of Commons ?"—" 14, Bucking- ham-street, Strand, W.C.—Dear venture to ask you to give the ' People's League ' your sympathy and support. You will see by enclosed question that the ' League ' does not attack a Second Chamber, but doee oppose the hereditary principle in legislatien, which, as you are aware, has been the great impediment in the way of real reform.—Faithfully yours, JOSEPH FORSTER, SeErerary." GREAT FIRE IN LEEDS £20,000 DnaloEs.—Early on Tuesday morning, for its duration, one of the most devas- tating tires broke out which has occurred in Leeds. Shortly after two o'clock, the extensive oil warehouses in Wood- house-lane, occupied by Messrs. Humble and Co., were dis- covered to be In flames. The premises contained a large stock of oil and similarly inflammable substances. When once the fire had got firm hold on the property, its salvation was Practically beyond human compass. The probabilities are that the tire originated on the St. Col umba-streeteide, for here, in its earlier stages, it raged with most vigour. By half-past twe the flames had got a firm hold of all the ware- ' houses—the single-storeyed ones near to St. Columba-street and Itockingham-,treet, and a three-storeyed structure near to Woodhouse-lane. The fire threw out a very strong glare, which must have been noticeable for miles. The tenants of all the houses adjoining bad left their beds and were look- ing to the safety of their persons and property,. Luckily the fire was restricted sufficiently to place the domestic com- forts of the occupants in no danger. The spectators re- mained in the street tilt the channels were filled with oil and water, and emitted a strong smell, and till the fire had almost burnt itself out, and the charred building looked huge and dark as they could be seen by the light of the dy- ing tire through the gaping roofs and windows. The confla- gration lasted in all not more than an hour. The damage amounted to £20,000.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THIIRSDAX.

The Queen at Balmoral van have her faithful daughter and her daughter's faithful husband amongst her constant guests. They will exchange the seclusion of Osborne for the seclusion of Bal- moral, as a confused convert once explained that he had renounced the errors of the Church of Rome and adopted those of the Church of England. Her Majesty in the Highlands keeps up a singular mix- ture of privacy and state. Amongst her attendants and ladies of state she is very exacting, but I am told she has rather a fussy way of visiting cottages and calling upon the neighbouring peasantry. In these kind-hearted and well-intentioned raids she has for years been accompanied by the Princess who will now have a new. presentation to make to her highland friends. The Queen and her daughter hold very opposite dpinions about the attractions of Balmora. The Princess always dreaded that autumn pilgrimage to the north, and preferred the Isle of Wight even to Windsor. The present con- ditions will be more pleasant for her, and it is very generally thought that the influence of the Princess will lead the Queen to be a little less unsecial when she returns to England. I hear that the Duke of Connaught is most anxious to return to India where his popularity was great y and where he had more authority and more responsibility than at home. If he goes it is likely it will be to take the chief com- mand of the Bombay army, succeeding General Har- cliiage who is now commander-in-chief. In politics during the week interest has chiefly centred on Ireland. It looks as if Dublin Castle were doomed, and Lord Carnarvon would have no successor as a Viceroy. His popularity has, however, been very great, and it is mainly due to a kind of casual heartiness and simplicity of manner which very much takes the Irish. His visit was a greater success than he himself expected, and he is entitled to more praise than he is likely to get, from one fact that had not been sufficiently appreciated. He really was very ill when he started on his excursion, and if the sea had not been unusually calm it might have been serious for him. A minister who succeeds a minister who has failed will always have some hostile critics, and Lord Carnarvon's; I won't say enemies, but unfriends, are complainingthat he was too civil and too conciliating. It was said of Lord Carlisle one day he was absent from a flower show that his laundress had got a new mangle, and that the Viceroy had gone to" open it." But Lord Car- narvon is not at all a man of the Howard type. He is amiable and he is affable, but all the time he is a diplomatist and a statesman. It is perhaps a% fit time now for the London Streets to be overhauled and undermined. Only what we gain by the absence of traffic we lose from the presence of a most aggravating thermometer. During the first few days of the week the Strand has been mephitic. Coal gas coming from sewers is easily confounded with sewer gas itself, and now that we are daily expecting cholera very little goes a long way in creating alarm. Bad smells, hot weather, and Covent Garden reeking with vegeta- able,ref use, prognosticates what we all dread. I understand that the question of the Gordon monument is a trouble to Mr. Plunkett. He is one of the few members of the Lower House whose seat is perfectly safe, otherwise he might be troubled with political matters of m6re personal concern. Also, he is one of the few members of the Lower House who believes that six months hence he will be found bn the same bench he occupied three weeks ago. What is to be done about Gor- don? The truth is, we ,have not a sculptor living who is worthy of the work. The dearth of genius is the main cause; but photography has a great deal to answer for. All our sculptors have now got into a rule of thumb way of producing a bust from three or four "photos ;" the likeness is certainly attained, but artistic quality is not even sought. That Belt case showed to what an extent the mechanical rules over the studio. Now Gordon's is a difficult face for a sculptor. Those who have known him will readily admit that what was heroic in the man, a brighten- ing of the eye, a fine manly penetrating glance, a countenance that changed expression and yet that never looked undecided, a sort of presence of re- source remaining as the paramount suggestion of the features, all this was entirely missed by the photographers. And how can a sculptor, however eminent—and we have now since Foley's death no really eminent sculptor—give this effect when pho- tography is his only aid? The noble points in such heads as Tennyson's, Byron's, Bonaparte's could not indeed well be missed, but Gordon's is too difficult and too subtle for the mediocrity which now usurps this branch of art. We have so many failures clus- stered round about Parliament that Mr. Plunket is scarcely to be blamed if, while fully admitting, and indeed insisting that Gordon should have a statue, he hesitates and is anxious about the selec- tbn of the executant • I have spoken of the streets of London all ripped up ; the parks are almost as bad. I never remember to have known the trees so barren of leaves while we are still in the month of August. The sun has been hot and perhaps there is some rain due to us., It has been what is called an old-fashioned August, but the state of the trees in Kensington Gardens is not to be thus explained. It is the elms that seem to have, chiefly suffered, and the decay is like a blight. Some localities have escaped, but in others and especially near the Round Pond opposite the Palace the mortality or rather the decrepitude seems very great. My own theory is that the cause is due not to sun, or drought, or smoke, but that the mischief lies lower down. It is not Lon- don air but London clay that causes the trouble. A geological map of Kensington Gardens, indeed of the whole West End, would show us this. Every- one has heard that the health of Kensington is due to its being built on gravel. When builders dig the foundations of a house they generally come oh. gravel, which is advertised for sale, and I am told that it has been known that a builder bought ground in order to sell it, and thus show that his house had a healthy substratum. But however thick the gravel may lie you have only to dig down a little lower to come upon the well- known London clay. Geologists call this blue gault, and it underlies all the London gravel. In Kensing- ton Gardens a section of the ground would show, first, a stratum of loam, then a bed of gravel, last the blue gault. This is so dense and so innutritious that the oak is the only tree whose roots will pierce it and live in it. All other trees rot the moment their roots reach this fatal layer. Here there is the ex- planation of so many of the Kensington elms be- ginning, as haircutters would say, to grow trim on the top. The gault is at varying depths, and so is reached in some quarters of the park sooner than in others. The elm trees planted by King William when he tried to reproduce in Rensington his favourite Holland, throve and flourished so long as their roots had only to deal with fresh loam and porous gravel. In our day, unfortunately; in their downward course they have come upon the gault, and all growth is arrested. Sooner or later, and in some cases very soon indeed, the elms of Kensing- ton will tumble down if they are not previously re- moved. I notice, however, that planting is going on extensively, and so the young trees will be ready to succeed the old ones.

When Londoners come back to town they will find new friends or at least new façades in old thoroughfares. I gave some time ago an account of the splendid file of buildings being erected in Coventry-street, on the site of the old Pavilion Music Hall. Day and night by sunshine and elec- tricity the contractors' men have been at work, and It is to be hoped that all will be ready by October. In the meantime there has been the pulling down of buildings as well as the running of them up. Op- posite the Criterion Theatre there was a very sorry row of houses let out to tobacconists, oyster dealers, at hose genus opine. Thoe are coming down, and are to ome down. I think from their debris one can learn that the jerry builder belongs to all time. It would be a great matter if they were not to be re- built. One could well dispense with that little delta of brick work. But I believe this is not to be. Lon- don space in the neighbourhood of Piccadilly Circus is much too valuable. Notwithstanding the rapidity with which the revised version of the Bible came forth from the printers there have been singularly few printers' errors. By this time there has been plenty of op- rrity to test and stody, and the printers would reto be 'communicated with the moment a blunder was detected. In old times there was need of stimulus to get people to be interested enough, and there was a tradition that the first person who pointed out a blunder received from the authorities at the University Press the sum of a guinea for the -service he had rendered. There have been many competitors for the guinea on this occasion, but as it was never promised I believe it has not been paid. The blunders that have been discovered up to this are quite unimportant, " righteous " spelled with the e left out, "shafts" with the t and f trans- posed, and the Ford " everflowing " printed "over- flowing." No pioint of doctrine is jeopardised by these errata—one might even read without noticing. There is no parallel to that verse in the Psalms,

"Printers have persecuted me without a cause," which indeed proved to be true. At the theatres there is little novelty. "Hood- mans Blind is a money success. Notwithstanding the heat the house is fairly full, and the play runs much better than it did the first night. In this kind of play the scenery needs to be rehearsed more than the acting. I think Wilson Barrett will make money of his piece, but he certainly loses rank. Better things were expected of him. His Hamlet was certainly not poetical, but at least it was orig- inal, and it was thoughtful. This sensation kind of business with a villain, a husband, a lovely faithful wife, virtue triumphant, and happiness before the curtain falls is unworthy of the manager who played "Claudian" and "The. Silver King." By . .. .

the way, I hear that the last piece is to be bi:oughl out at the Ambigu, in Paris, under the singularly inappropriate title of "Le Roi d'Argent." We have borrowed so much, and so much that is unhealthy from the French, that it is quite a pleasure to send them over a good wholesome play. A greater play even than "The Silver King" is now being rehearsed for the forthcoming season. At the Theatre Fran- cais "Hamlet " 'is to be produced, and that most hysterical of all French actors, Mounet-Sully, a . . .

Bleckley and 'Joseph Davies, Sir Gilbert was requested, along with all the other leading gentry of the district, to allow his name to be added to the local committee as a supporter of the ship canal scheme. Sir Gilbert veiy promptly perused to have anything to do 'wit) the matter. So tar, I believe, he has not subscribed a sMgle peuay , towards the vast expenditure which the successful prose( u- tion of the ship canal scheme has entziled upon the promo- ' tere ; but more than this, when that magnificent vote (I use !Dr. Mackie's description) was taken et toe ratepayers of IWarringtota, in favour of subscribing £l,OOO out of the borough rates towards the expenses of promoting the bill lin Parliament, the votini, papers of Gremall, Whitley and Co., Limited, and of Sir Gilbert Greenall, were returned lunfilled up. This is another proof of the real interest Sir Gil- bert takes in anything which is calculated te benefit our town. So well acquainted with these facts were many of the persons present at the meeting that the coolness of Sir Gilbert's reception was a fitting rebuke. As a Liberal, lam not sorry that Sir Gilbert "spoke "at the meeting, for a more pitiable'exhibition of unfittedness for the position of a-member for Parliament It would be difficult to imagine. It is an insult t 0 the intelleet!of the town to offer such a candidate for our suffrages.—Yours,
SHIP CANAL.

At the Borough Court, yesterday morning, " Pro- f essor " Smythe, a coloured man, who carries on business in Winwick-street and the Market as a herbalist, summoned Ur. Fletcher, of Runcorn, a rival herbalist, who has a place of business in War- rington Market, and James Barrett, an assistant of his, for an assault alleged to have been committed in the Market oa Saturday, the 22nd inst.—Mr. A Browne appeared for the complainant, and Mr. P. Davies represented the defendants.—ln his opening statement, Mr. Browne said that the asstkult WAS only of a technical character, but such a one as might lead to a serious disturbance in tha Market. Com- plainant sold botanic beer and other things, and Mr. Fletcher was a rival herbalist. On the Saturday afternoon in question his client was reading—ap- parently from a newspaper—to a crowd surrounding his stall. Whilst he was so doing defendant Barrett came up and said " bet you 55 what you are reading is not in the paper.' Complainant would have nothing to do with him, but Barrett again came and offered to bet a sovereign on the same subject. He then challenged Smythe to fight. Fletcher came out of his shop, pushed Barrett away, and, going towards Smythe. called him a " black dog" and a "black villain." He was 'then about to rush at Smythe, when a market porter arrested his progress by placing some hampers in the way before him. There was a great disturbance, and a policeman had to be called. Complainant bore out the opening statement of his advocate, and, in answer to Mr. Davies. he said that he was a " professor " of botany and an herbalist, and had had 20 years' experience. In reply to the quesdon had he any right to the title of professor, he said that there were hundreds and thousands who called themselves " pro- fessors." He denied having said that Mr. Fletcher, who wore a uniform and half-a-dozen medals, had

not been a soldier, and had lost his arm in a mill. A number of witnesses were called to prove the assault, and Mr. Davies, in his speech for the defence, said that Mr. Fletcher was a respect- able man, and had a diploma, which was examined in court. Complainant, who was a native of Calcutta, came to the market and took a stall close to the front door of Mr. Fletcher's shop. Smythe told the people openly in the market that Fletcher ,was a humbug, had purchased his medals, and had not lost his arm in battle. In reality Mr. Fletcher lost his arm at Alma, and had served in other celebrated engage- ments. It was denied that any assault had been com- mitted, and witnesses were called to prove the irrita- ting conduct of the complainant. It was also men- tioned that Mr. Fletcher was 80 esteemed in Runcorn that recently the townspeople evinced their rtAgard by presenting him with a handsome gold watch and ehaio.--The magistrates, after hearing the facts of the matter, dismissed the case.

The band was composed of the following local musicians :—Violins, Mr. R.. H. Pearson (leader), Mr. P. Caldwell, Mr. T. Bancroft; Mr. H. Bond; double basso, Mr. "W. Charnock ; flute, Sergt.-Drummer W. Burgess ; cornet,Sergeant- Drummer O'Brien; second cornet, Mr. J. Podmore ; trombone, Mr. IL Anderton ; piano, Mr. T. Ford: harmonium, Mr. F. Booth. Mr. W. S. Woods acted as conductor, and it is due to him and the orchestra to say that so far as they were concerned the per- formance was exceptionally good. The opera con- tains some really charming music, and it is alto- gether so bright and "taking" that it is surprising that it has gone out of print. It is much superior to some operettas that have recently, been put upon the stage. The parts for the band required to be orchestrated from the piano score, and this impor- tant work has, we learn, been most efficiently exe- cuted by Mr. B. W. Manning. 'Miss Wallington and Miss Monks—the ladies who had parts in "Pun- chinello "—may now be regarded as professional vocalists, but this was their first appearance in opera, and it is pleasing to be able to say that they surpassed themselves. As Babette, Miss Monks was the first to present herself, and it was soon seen that she was equal to her task. She was, comparatively speak- , ing, easy in manner, and sang throughout with ' steadiness, and, occasionally, something of dramatic power. She treated the audience to a delightful rendering of the Sabot song, and, if she could only have emphasised the clic-clac with the sabots, she would have brought down the house. Miss Wal-. lington was not less successful as Violette. She was in excellent voice, and sang with confidence and precision. It was a great treat to hear her render the ballad " Coo,' says the gentle dove," which was loudly applauded. She was not less effective in the concerted pieces; and it is not too much to say that the two "weaker vessels" showed themselves much superior to the so-called "superior sex." Mr. J. T. Picton had a heavy role as Polichenelle, and it seemed at times to overtax him, somewhat. This was most perceptible in "The Showman's Ditty." He showed himself in other respects thoroughly master of his part, and revealed high:histrionic ability in the final scene. Mr. Pickmere " looked " the Marquis admirably, but he was too constrained—probably by anxiety as to his vocalism —to make the most of the part. He succeeded best in the comedy of the serenade scene, and sang the serenade itself fairly well. Mr. Jenkins was, rather unequal as Agamem- non ; he, however, distinguished himself, both as to singing and acting, in the duet with Miss Wallington, " High-born beauty, canst thou leave." Mr. Leg- horn's Vignolles was very praiseworthy.; and the chorus, which was a powerful one, sang well. The new costumes, supplied by Mr. James Carr, were really brilliant, and the opera was altogether well mounted. It was considerably after eleven o'clock on Thursday night when the curtain fell on an entertainment which had been much enjoyed. Last night there was again a large and fashion- I able attendance, and the performance all through was a marked improvement upon that of Thurs- day. Miss Wallington was encored for her render- ! ing of "Coo,' says the gentle dove," and both Miss Wallington and Miss Monks were presented with bouquets. We learn from Mr. A. Woods. the hon. I sec., that as the result of the two performances there will be a good round sum to hand over to the funds of the Infirmary.

Sir,—ls it true that the Wilderepooi Brewery folk have just given the job of building the new Roebuck to a Man- 'cheater man? If it is correct, then my vote goes Liberal this time, for I cannot help remembering how we walked about wanting work when Walton Church was building for the same reason as now exists as regards the present job. I suppose this is another Instance of Sir Gilbert's friend- ship for the working-men of Warrington. Re gets his money here, and spends it somewhere else.—l am. sir, yours respectfully,

div.head: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS ELECTION.
div.p: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS ELECTION.

Sir,--t see from your paper we are to buys an election of Commissioners neat week. I have not yet heard of any gentlemen offeriog themselves as candidates; but as a resi- dent in Duke's Field, feeling that this end of the town, which contains so many Inhabitants as well as owners of cottages, should be fully represented on the Board of COM. missioners, I trust the ratepayers in the Field will see that they have one if not two representatives. We want our streets sweeping and watering. We pay a large amount in rates, but we cannot get these requirements attended to. I would suggest that a number of the property owners and ratepayers In the field meet to consider the matter at once.— Yours truly, DUKB'S FIELD. Duke's Field, Runcorn, August 27th, 1985

MILE DEALERS AND THE PRICE OF MILK. 81r,— rite Warrington milk dealers as a body have decided to have milk at a cheaper rate during the winter months. Our motto is Live and let live ;" but the price we have been paving the east winters has not given us a chance to live. Upon inquiry we find that we are giving considerably more than the milk dealers In Liverpo.l and Manchester, who are getting 44 per quart for their milk. Many of the Cheshire farmers are only getting Is Oland is 7d per dozen after paying railway expenses, and then there is the wear and ter of their tankard's, which is sometimes a consider- able Item in their expenditure. Already several of the milk dealers have made arrangements with their farmers for the supply of milk during the winter months at the same price as they are now wing. viz: 2s per dozen. As a body we consider that to be a lair price, winter and summer, and have all decided not to give any mere.—Youre &c., .
A MILE 'DEALER.

' THE RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY. Sir,—The well-timed letter of 't Biblioth,que " in your current issue is a source of unveiled delight and buoyant hope to a great number of borrowers from the above insti- tution. Will you kindly, with your usual and expansive sympathy with all persons who are subjected to an unneces- sary amount of redtapiern, allow me to second and empha- size the vigorous protest against the unscrupulous favourit- ism exhibited in this lending library systematically. Icm confirm from personal k.trwledge the tam that about a score of favoured personages have the privileged entry into the library enclosure, and think it high time that the facilities of the library should be offered alike to all persons whose names are on the roll, and not that the affluent who are otherwise able to obtain books should have the inestimable Privilege of entering, and chooting for themselves. The library committee would he none the worse for an increased exercise of vigour and vigilance, and may look out for squalls undoubtedly (and what is worse, find them :1 at the next election, if the trust imposed on them of providing an institution for the chief use of those who/cannot obtain literature elsewhere for indigence, is so misused as to bring good to the richer few at the exuertee of the peor. It would save much trouble and annoyance if the committee would issue a dictum that the carrying out of the library rules, verbatim et literatintis compulsory. It seems in all pub- lic offices rules are all one-sided, and work against the people for the benefit of the officers ; or at any rate that a cede of rules is like pie crust, made solely to be broken. A little of disinterested conduct of the affairs of small Im- port, but which are very near and dear to elect6-s, would not. I am assured, be thrown away for the election time. Roping that this matter will not be allowed to pies away entirely unnoticed, as already malgre " Bibliotheque's." , letters the " favoured " have been admitted this week, still 'to the detriment of the mass of borrowers, and with all lost wisbes for the success of your influential (and increasingly so) paper,—l remain, yours, dtc,, BIENVENU.
