----- The Duchess of Alb my, with family and suite, arrived at Llandudno on Friday morning. Mr. Collins, editor of " The Schoolmaster," has been se- lected the Liberal candidate for Camberwell (Dulwich Divi- sion). .
Austria has declared ten days' quarantine on arrivals from Gibraltar in consequence of alleged prevalence of cholera there.

Notwithstanding the rainy weather, an immense crowd collected on the Esplande of the Invalides. Paris, on Friday, to witness the funeral of the late Admiral Courber. Mr. Ruskin, who has been lying ill at Brentwood, is so much better that Dr. Gesrge Parsons, his medical adviser, considers it unnecessary to issue any further bulletin. At Tralee, on Friday, Patrick Moriarty, a sergeant in the Kerry Militia, caretaker on an evicted farm, was coin- mitted for trial for tiring a revolver at four young ladies.

Owing to a rush among a great crowd of visitors to the Eisteddfod at the Great-Western Station, Aberdare,on Thurs- day night, a woman named Sansoin, from Devonshire, was pushed over the platform and killed by a train. THE OLDHAM STRIKE.—The Ol4hau2 strike completed its sixth week on Friday, and as yet there is not the slight- est sign of a settlement. It is stated that after the wakes the mills will be re-opened, to give an opportimity of resuming work. The percentage of unionists en strike is 65 13.

THE MARQUIS OF RIPON.—The Marquis of Ripon has promised to address a meeting in St. Helens on the 15th proximo,in aid of the funds of the Sr. Helens Providence Hospital, an institution founded and worked by Catholic Sisters. Both Liberal and Conservative candidates for the borough are to be present._

FATAL COLLAPSE OF A BRIDOE.—AB the men employed in the erecion of a new high level bridge which crosses the Barrow Docks were preparing to leave work on Thursday night the whole of one of the archway, about thirty yards long, fell in without any warning. James Lappin, aged twenty-two years, who was working on the top of the arch- way at the time, was crushed to death amongst the ruins. ir..t.arGgn Munnen IN GLASGOW.—On Friday Alexander Macintyre, aged 27 years, labourer, was remanded at Glas- gow Police Court. On Thursday night he quarrelled with a hawker named James M'Dermid, in King-street, Glasgow. In his rage he threw a bottle at the head of M.'Derrnid, in- dicting a fearful gash. Nl' ermid fell to the ground, and was carried to the infirmary, where he died. Macintyre, who was under the icfluence of drink at the time he mur- dered the man, now feels his po4tion keenly. The OLIVER PAIN AGITATION. A largely attended meeting of Anglo-Frenchmen, Frenchmen resident in Lon- don and visiting the metropolis, was held at the Hotel de Strangers, Leicester-square, on Friday. The action of Rochefort and others was strongly denounced, and a resolu- tion was passed with only one dissentient expressing in- dignation at the outrageous language used by a smell revo- lutionary section in Paris, in connection with the Oliver Pain affair, repudiating all sympathy with such proceed- ings, and setting forth the .villingness of the meeting to let the matter rest with the administrative oarthorities of Ragland and France. RUMOURED ROYAL MARRIAGE.

COPENHAGEN, FRlDAY.—Rumours of a marriage between Prince Oscar of Sweden and the eldest dauglyter of the Prince of Wales are more prevalent here than ever, notwith- standing a telegram of denial from Stockholm. _ THE CZAR'S RETURN.

div.head: MAYOR "AT HOME."
div.p: THE MAYOR "AT HOME."

From three to six o'clock on the afternoon of Thursday the Mayor of Warrington, Alderman Har- rison, held an "At Home "at the Town Hall. Not- withstanding that the weather was cold and gloomy, with a drizzling rain, a large number attended to pay their respects to his Worship and the lady Mayoress. The reception was held in the Council Chamber, which was pretty with floral decorations. There was a constant flow of visitors, who were announced by Mr. Dennett, the hall keeper, who acted as usher. In the entrance hall were arranged a number of plants, placed there by Mr. Green, the head gardener. The state of the weather prevented indulgence in lawn tennis, but the guests, while chatting one with another, or partaking of the light refreshments pro• vided, were beguiled with sweet music from without, which was discoursed by the bands of the Blue Coat School and Padgate Industrial School. Afterwarals the members of these bands had a share of the good things provided, being regaled with tea in the kitchen underneath the hall. Invitation had been issued by advertisement to one and all, and the Mayor and Mayoress assiduously attended to their guests. Amongst those who were present or sent cards were the following :—Rev. RUNCORN, WESTON, AND HALTON WATER- WORKS COMPANY. The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of this com- pany was held at the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Monday afternoon. Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., chairman of directors, presided, and there were present—Messrs. W. Hayes, J. Simpson, E. Timmins, T. Bankes, T. Norman, J. Collier, P. Smith, J. Shaw, W. F. Salkeld (secretary), and W. Jones.—The Secretary read the directors' report which was published in last Saturday's Examincr.—The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report and balance sheet and the payment of a dividend of 31 per cent, per annum free of income tax, remarked that alrlaouo this dividend was less than that paid at the Christmas half-year, it was at the 84030 mom that paid in the corresponding half of 1834. The serious depression in trade had affected the waterworks by the stoppage of the Smelting works and the Glycerine worse, which had paid the company something like £4OO a year. Other large works had partially stopped and de- creased their consumption of water, and all this told very materially upon the, profits of toe company. The directors. had reduced the expenditwe considerably. They had saved £6O on the interest on debentures and preference stock, had reduced the wages by 111549, and had made a con- tract for 'coal which would save them 8d per ton. Its re- ferred with gratification to the fact that the water bill in- troduced by Lord Camperdown had not passed, and said the directors had joined the Provincial Waterworks Associa- tion fat the purpose of opposing the bill should it be again introduced, and for watching any future measures that might be brought into Parliament affecting the Waterworks Clauses Act. In conclusion he hoped that with a revival of trade, and the decrease cS expenses he had shown, the company would be able to declare a better dividend in the future.—Mr. T. liatikes seconded the motion.--Mr. P. Smith said he understood that in other towns the large manufactories could obtain water cheaper than. could the manufactories in Runcorn, and if the water could be re- duced from seyenpence to sixpence he belieeed the com- pany would have a far greater consampition. In his opinion water companies like other bireiriese concerns should be open to competition,—The Chairman replied that the water could not be sold at a profit for sixpence, and IMr. Timmins said he did not think the's-wero any water- works in the country that had to pump the water by steam engines that sold water at a less rate than Runcorn.—Mr. Smith said of course it would be absurd to sell at a loss.— The report was adopted .—On the motion of Mr T. Norman, secon led by Mr. Shaw, Messrs. Hayes and Simpson were reelected directors. Mr. Robert Flonikes was re-appointed auditor on the motion of Mr. Collier, A vote of thanks was accorded to the directors on the motion of Mr. T. Norman (who regretted that the funds would not permit of their be- ing paid for their arduous labours, seconded by Mt. Shaw, and the chairman having replied the meeting con. eluded.

HAGUE'S MINSTRELS.—Mr. Sam Hague's talented minstrel troupe will appear in the Public Hall, en Monday and Tuesday evenings. The programme to , be gone through is of a varied and entertaining description, and no doubt its execution will be such as to maintain the very high reputation of Mr. Hague's company. SPURIOUS Co.—The public generally should lust now be specially on their guard against receiv- ing bad coin; as we understand there is a consider- able quantity in circulation. Florins and half- crowns seem the most common, and several spuri- ous ones are in the possession of the police, who are no doubt keeping a sharp look out to detect the offenders. PADISHEAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL. On Sunday evening the Rev.. Robert Dillon preached his fares well sermon in the above chapel to a large congre- gation. He took the text from Acts, chapter 20th, verse 32nd, "Brethren / now commend you to GM." The sermon was impressive and suitable for thEroc.. casion. Mr. Dillon has been in Cadishead circuit three years, and is about to remove to an appoint- ment in the city of Dbrcbester. The rev. gentlemanl will be followed by the. good wishes and earnest prayers of a large circle of friends to whom he has endeared himself by his three years' ministry and pastoral intercourse. It is a great satisfaction to• him to know that he leaves the church in al very prosperous spiritual condition. AN EMPLOYEE& ExctrusioN.—The annual excur-, sion of the employees cof Messrs. P. Walker and Sons, brewers, Warrington, took place on Saturday to Southport. About 400 proceeded by the train which left the Central Station at half-past nine, and reached Southport at half-past ten. Special arrange- ments had been made as to admission to the Winter Gardens and other prates of interest, and these were consequently extensively' visit ed. The excursion safely arrived back at Warrington about nine o'clock, though several og the trippers made use of the extension tickets and stayed at Southport till , Monday and Tuesday. Messrs. Walker and Sons generously gave each workman a railway ticket, a day's wages, and half-a-crown as pocket money. BOWLING MATCH AT GuiPPENHALL.—The bowl- ing green attached to the Dog and Dart Inn, Grap- penhall, was the scene of a lively contest on Satur- day afternoon, when W. Webster (alias 'Tom Hart '),and R. Fairbrother, both of Warrington, played a game of bowls, 21 up, for £2 a side, the latter giving "the champion " three points start. Fairbrother was the first to score, but after making a couple and a single in. the first two ends, he was unable to hold his Owe, as Webster commenced playing in better form, and never gave his oppo- nent a chance until the game was called 19 to 18 in his favour. Fairbrother was unable to take the op- portunity, and at tiie•next end 'the champion" won the game by playing one against the jack. The scores at the finish of thegame were :—Webster, 21; Fairbrother, 18. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE 01719-ARRINGTON. —For week ending Saturday, Aug. 22nd, 1885.—The ' mean teraperature was 57 Fahr., and therefore 2i degrees warmer-than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 70,Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 16th inst., and the minimum temperature. 40 Fahrenheit, on the 19th inst. The rainfall measured lin. The. general direction of the wind was east. During the week, which was the 34th of the current year,.2B births and 12 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 131 per 1,000, against 13.9 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 30.3 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from diarrh&a,. 2 from phthisis, 1 from lung disease, 2 from brain disease, 1 from drowning, 1 run over by a railway wagon, and 1 cut throat. One case of typhus tever, 1 of typhoid fever, 1 of measles, and 2 of whooping cough were reported under the requirements of the Act of Par- liament.—JoHN IL GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.
